reference_title: Ground Modification Methods Reference Manual – Volume II

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Introduction to subgrade stabilization methods for foundation support of pavement structural sections, grouped in three categories: mechanical stabilization, admixture (chemical) stabilization and stabilization through moisture control, with the common technologies listed in Tables 9-1 to 9-3.
sections.body: The chapter reviews subgrade stabilization methods for foundation support of pavement structural sections (surface asphalt or concrete pavement, base and subbase layers) (p. 9-1). Proper treatment of problem soil conditions and preparation of the pavement foundation are extremely important for a long-lasting pavement that does not need excessive maintenance. When compaction alone will not improve the subgrade, or may make it worse, the conventional technique is to remove and replace poor subgrade soils with better compacted materials (a form of mechanical stabilization); this is not always the most economical or desirable treatment because excavation can create disturbance and removal and disposal problems. Other stabilization technologies can be more effective in improving strength and modulus for construction and performance. They fall into three categories: (1) mechanical stabilization using thick granular layers, blending with more competent materials, geosynthetics (geotextiles, geogrids) with granular layers, or lightweight fill; (2) admixture stabilization of weak soils with chemical agents (lime, cement, asphalt, fly ash or other admixtures); (3) stabilization through moisture control (dewatering, drainage or moisture barrier). The most common technologies in each category are listed in Tables 9-1 (mechanical, p. 9-2), 9-2 (admixture/additive, p. 9-3) and 9-3 (moisture control, p. 9-3), all from Rollings and Rollings (1996). Table 9-1 lists thicker gravel, blending, geosynthetics, lightweight fill and recycled material; Table 9-2 lists Portland cement, lime, lime-fly ash, lime-cement-fly ash, bituminous, pozzolanic and slags and other chemical admixtures; Table 9-3 lists improved drainage and partial and full encapsulation.
key_points: Three categories of pavement support stabilization: mechanical, admixture (chemical) and moisture control (p. 9-1).
Remove-and-replace is the conventional technique but excavation can cause disturbance and disposal problems.
Table 9-1 (p. 9-2): thicker gravel reduces the dynamic stress level on silts and clays; geosynthetics on silts and clays minimize disturbance and give strength gain through consolidation.
Table 9-2 (p. 9-3): lime on non-plastic soil gives no improvement (no reactive material); bituminous stabilization of fines cannot be mixed.
Table 9-3 (p. 9-3): improved drainage suits sand, silt and wet low plastic clays; encapsulation suits plastic and collapsible soils.

sections.title: Description
sections.summary: Why subgrade soils are stabilized for pavement support: a uniform stiffness, a construction platform over wet weak soils, strengthening and restricting volume change, and reducing moisture susceptibility of fine-grained soils.
sections.body: The most important consideration for any stabilization technique used for pavement support is a uniform soil stiffness (p. 9-4). The stiffness (resilient modulus) of some soils depends strongly on moisture and stress state; uniformity can be achieved by sub-cutting and recompacting the subgrade or by other stabilization techniques, and admixtures/additives can improve strength and stiffness. Stabilization may also improve workability (compactability), minimize strength and modulus loss due to moisture, reduce swelling and shrinkage of expansive materials, and mitigate frost heave. Subgrade soils are usually stabilized for three reasons: (1) to create a construction platform over or with (e.g., by drying) wet, weak soils, in which case the stabilized subgrade is not usually considered a structural layer, although guidance is given for assessing long-term improvement that can be considered in design; (2) to strengthen a weak soil and restrict the volume change potential of a highly plastic or compressible soil, in which case the soil is considered 'modified' and usually given some structural credit; (3) to reduce moisture susceptibility of fine-grained soils.
key_points: Uniform subgrade stiffness is the most important consideration for any pavement support stabilization (p. 9-4).
A construction-platform stabilization is not usually counted as a structural layer.
A 'modified' soil that is strengthened and volume-stable is usually given structural credit in pavement design.

sections.title: Mechanical Stabilization
sections.summary: Mechanical stabilization: replacing weak subgrade with compacted granular material, blending, geosynthetic separation and stabilization, lightweight fill and recycled materials; AASHTO identifies geosynthetic applications below about 2000 psf undrained strength (CBR about 3) as mechanical stabilization.
sections.body: Mechanical stabilization is the replacement of a thickness of weak subgrade with a more competent compacted material; if compaction alone gives suitable stiffness and uniformity no other method is needed (p. 9-4). Granular backfill (sand, gravel, crushed concrete, recycled asphalt) is often used, enhanced by geosynthetics; finer soils can be blended with granular material, and lightweight materials reduce the vertical stress on the subgrade. Thick granular layers (1.1.1.1) give a working platform; the layer must be thick enough that subgrade stress does not exceed its bearing capacity. The added thickness is usually not counted in design because fines (minus No. 200) can migrate up by pumping and contaminate it. Blending with gravel or recycled pavement creates a drier condition and reduces the influence of plasticity (p. 9-5). Geosynthetic separation (1.1.1.2), typically a geotextile beneath granular layers, prevents intermixing and is critical for open graded drainage layers; open graded coarse (e.g., 3-inch) angular aggregate over a separation geotextile is a very good draining layer for extremely soft wet subgrades; it should be considered for SC, CL, CH, ML, MH, OL, OH, PT (AASHTO A-5, A-6, A-7-5, A-7-6) soils. Geosynthetic stabilization (1.1.1.3) uses stronger geosynthetics to reduce gravel thickness; they must also separate and filter; AASHTO (2014a) identifies applications with undrained shear strength less than about 2000 psf (CBR about 3) as mechanical stabilization (p. 9-6). Lightweight fill (1.1.1.4) reduces stress and settlement over highly compressible soils (geofoam, foamed concrete, tire shreds, expanded shale and clay, fly ash, bottom ash, boiler slag, air-cooled slag). Recycled materials (1.1.1.5) are either reuse of pavement materials (RAP, RCM; rubblize and roll for PCC, full depth reclamation for AC) or recycled waste materials (pp. 9-6 to 9-7).
key_points: Thick granular layer must spread load so subgrade stress stays below its bearing capacity (p. 9-5).
Extra gravel thickness is usually not counted in design because fines contamination reduces strength, stiffness and drainage over time.
Separation geotextiles should be considered for SC, CL, CH, ML, MH, OL, OH and PT soils (A-5, A-6, A-7-5, A-7-6).
Geosynthetic stabilization applies where undrained shear strength is less than about 2000 psf (CBR about 3) (p. 9-6).
Rubblize and roll (PCC) and full depth reclamation (AC) are in-place recycling procedures (p. 9-7).

sections.title: Admixture (a.k.a. Chemical) Stabilization
sections.summary: Admixture stabilization with cement and cement kiln dust, lime, fly ash, asphalt and their combinations; mechanisms of void filling, particle coating, binding, cementing, flocculation and cation exchange.
sections.body: Stabilization with admixtures mixes the soil with lime, cement, fly ash, bitumen or proprietary chemical stabilizers (proprietary products are not covered) to control swelling and frost heave and improve strength (p. 9-7). Mechanisms include filling voids (reducing permeability), coating particles, binding particles (adding cohesive strength and resisting swelling), cementing by chemical reaction (lime, Portland cement), flocculation and cation exchange (p. 9-8). Cement (1.1.2.1): for low-plasticity clays, sandy and granular soils; low contents give cement-modified soil, higher contents soil-cement or cement-treated base/subbase/subgrade; too high a content can cause shrinkage cracking. Cement kiln dust: pre-calciner dust has higher free lime and performs more like lime; long-kiln dust has more calcium carbonate (Parsons et al. 2004). Lime (1.1.2.2): most effective in improving workability and reducing swell of highly plastic clays with montmorillonite, illite and kaolinite, and to dry wet soils; hydrated lime as powder or slurry is used most. Fly ash (1.1.2.3): Class C (lignite or subbituminous coal, 'high lime') is self-cementing and pozzolanic; Class F (anthracite or bituminous coal, 'low lime') needs added lime; must meet ASTM C593 (p. 9-9). Asphalt (1.1.2.4): sand-bitumen, soil-bitumen and sand-gravel bitumen; durability assessed by water absorption; soils with fines in excess of 20% are not recommended. Combinations (1.1.2.5): lime-fly ash (LF) and lime-cement-fly ash (LCF) for coarse soils with little or no fines, often for base and subbase.
key_points: Lime is most effective on highly plastic clays containing montmorillonite, illite and kaolinite (p. 9-8).
Class C fly ash is self-cementing; Class F needs lime; fly ash for stabilization must meet ASTM C593 (p. 9-9).
Asphalt treatment of soils with fines in excess of 20% is not recommended (p. 9-9).
LF and LCF combinations suit coarse-grained soils with little or no fines.

sections.title: Moisture Control
sections.summary: Moisture control by dewatering with underdrains and cutoff drains, geosynthetic and geocomposite drainage, and partial or full encapsulation of moisture sensitive soils.
sections.body: Moisture control should always be incorporated in pavement design and may be needed before and during construction to stabilize moisture sensitive soils; it can be classical dewatering with trench or horizontal blanket drains (the latter a capillary cap and frost heave control) or prevention of moisture change by encapsulation (p. 9-9). Improved drainage-dewatering (1.1.3.1): underdrains on new projects and cleaned outlets on rehabilitation projects typically reduce pumping within a few days. Soils subject to densification and not free draining (saturation exceeding 80-90%) within 2 to 4 feet of the surface are not expected to support construction traffic; saturated soils with more than 10% fines are not expected to be drainable for construction traffic, and evaporation (disking, aeration) may be more feasible; cutoff drains keep groundwater out (p. 9-10). Geosynthetic drainage (1.1.3.2): prefabricated geocomposite drains (cores with geotextile filters) replace or support conventional drains; thick needle-punched nonwovens give some in-plane drainage; drainage geosynthetics at the subgrade-stabilization interface can drain the subgrade under dense graded aggregate or speed drainage of the aggregate. Partial and full encapsulation (1.1.3.3) keeps fine-grained soils at or slightly below optimum moisture; by 1998 more than 100 projects worldwide were identified, usually reporting success with expansive soils (Steinberg 1998) (p. 9-11).
key_points: Soils with saturation exceeding 80-90% within 2 to 4 ft of the surface are not expected to support construction traffic (p. 9-10).
Saturated soils with more than 10% fines are not expected to be drainable for construction traffic.
Encapsulation keeps fine-grained soils at or slightly below optimum moisture content (p. 9-11).

sections.title: Alternate Technologies
sections.summary: Other technologies for pavement support: geogrid and geotextile base reinforcement, geocells, bio-treatment, electro-osmosis and vacuum consolidation beneath existing pavements.
sections.body: Geogrids and geotextiles can reinforce the base course of flexible pavement, especially thin pavements on secondary roads (p. 9-11). Geocells, three-dimensional honeycomb geosynthetics confining granular materials, were developed with the US Army Corps of Engineers for roadway stabilization (Webster and Watkins 1977, Webster 1979, 1981); cost has been the main deterrent, but they allow reduced base thickness and longer service life (Yang et al. 2013, Thakur et al. 2012, Han et al. 2011). Bio-treatment uses chemical and biological reactions; it is more complex than admixtures and depends on temperature, pH, donor and acceptor concentrations and nutrient diffusion (DeJong et al. 2010, Mitchell and Santamarina 2005, Ivanov and Chu 2008) (p. 9-12). For existing pavements where traffic cannot be disrupted, electro-osmosis (pore water movement under electric potential, for low permeability silts and clays, with simple equipment and low mobilization cost) and vacuum consolidation (pavement sealed with a bitumen coated geotextile or removable geomembrane extended into an edge trench, vacuum applied through the trench and base) remove moisture beneath the pavement. More information is in GeoTechTools.
key_points: Geocells were developed with the US Army Corps of Engineers for roadway stabilization (p. 9-11).
Electro-osmosis and vacuum consolidation can stabilize subgrades under existing pavements without removing them (p. 9-12).

sections.title: Historical Overview
sections.summary: History of roadway stabilization: ancient gravel roads with reed mat separators and drainage, corduroy roads, admixtures from the 1960s, slag fills from about 1950, modern geosynthetics from the 1960s with USFS design methods in the early 1970s, and the AASHTO (2008) MEPDG.
sections.body: Stabilization methods have been used for thousands of years: ancient Roman roads used thick gravel, reed mats as separators and drainage, and corduroy roads (timbers roped or chained together) were used over soft ground in the 1800s (p. 9-12). Admixture stabilization began during the 1960s because of aggregate and petroleum shortages, fell out of favor by the 1980s through faulty application and inadequate design, and has since been improved by research, materials and equipment (p. 9-13). Wood fiber has long been used by timber companies over peat bogs; slag was crushed and sold for fill beginning around 1950. Geosynthetic type materials were first used in the 1920s and 1930s; modern polymeric geosynthetics in the 1960s, with design methods first advanced by the USFS for logging haul roads in the early 1970s; monitoring has shown benefits extending to long-term performance. The AASHTO (2008) Mechanistic Empirical Pavement Design Guide (MEPDG), though not fully developed for stabilization, has the potential to include the stabilization layer with calibrated degradation factors; calibration information is being developed by several state agencies.
key_points: Admixture stabilization began in the 1960s and regained acceptance over the past two decades (p. 9-13).
USFS advanced the first geosynthetic design methods for logging haul roads in the early 1970s.
The MEPDG could include a stabilization layer with calibrated degradation factors.
sections.applicability: Background on how stabilization practice developed.

sections.title: Comparison/Applicability of Stabilization Technologies
sections.summary: Comparing stabilization technologies: the need for a good subsurface exploration, Table 9-4 benefits matrix, and the relative merits of mechanical stabilization, admixtures, drainage and encapsulation.
sections.body: The largest geotechnical challenge is identifying the need for stabilization and having enough information to pick a method; conditions are often discovered during construction when it is too late to run the needed tests (p. 9-13). A good subsurface exploration should identify subgrade conditions along the alignment (FHWA 2010), and geophysics should be considered to locate areas needing stabilization (p. 9-14). Tables 9-1 to 9-3 and Table 9-4 (benefits of each method, p. 9-15) help determine applicability; state flow charts usually cover only one type (e.g., chemical). Mechanical stabilization works immediately (no curing); geosynthetics with gravel maintain gravel integrity and may give long-term subgrade strength gain; free draining material with geosynthetics improves drainage and frost protection; disadvantages are excavation and disposal and the need for quality granular material. Admixtures give in-place improvement of strength, modulus and durability and mitigate swell or frost heave in some combinations, but need up-front lab testing, good field control and a curing time of three to seven days, have dust and weather issues, and caution is advised with organics or sulfates. Drainage should always be the first technique to apply/try and is the least costly, but some soils drain very slowly; full encapsulation can mitigate swelling soils; partial encapsulation needs no excavation but is not permanent.
key_points: Geophysics should be considered to locate areas requiring stabilization along a roadway (p. 9-14).
Mechanical stabilization works immediately; admixtures need a curing time of three to seven days.
Caution with admixtures where soils contain organics or sulfates.
Drainage should always be the first technique to apply/try and is the least costly.

sections.title: Focus and Scope
sections.summary: Scope of the chapter: overview of common subgrade stabilization methods for pavement construction on marginal soils, with suitability, improvement, advantages, limitations, design parameters, specifications, quality assurance and cost.
sections.body: The chapter presents an overview of the more common methods of stabilizing subgrade soils for pavement construction and improving the design life of pavements on marginal soils (p. 9-16). It reviews suitability for different soils, the improvement to be anticipated for construction and over the pavement life, and the advantages, disadvantages and limitations of each technology, with typical geotechnical design parameters and design and construction considerations. It also gives guidelines and references for specifications, suggested quality assurance including construction quality control, and cost information for estimating and comparing technologies.
sections.applicability: Understanding what the chapter covers.

sections.title: Glossary
sections.summary: Definitions of terms used for subgrade stabilization: base course, CBR, cement kiln dust, chemical and mechanical stabilization, geosynthetic types, encapsulation, lightweight fill, RAP, RCM, PGED, subgrade, subbase, vacuum preloading and others.
sections.body: The glossary defines terms used with subgrade stabilization methods, mostly after FHWA (2010) and FHWA (2008) (pp. 9-16 to 9-22). Selected definitions: California Bearing Ratio (CBR) - ratio of the force per unit area to penetrate a soil with a 3 square inch piston (about 2-inch diameter) at 0.05 inches/minute to that for a standard material; an index from 0 to 100, a very weak high plasticity clay having CBR 0 to 1 and a high quality well-graded crushed stone 100. Chemical stabilization - mixing lime, cement, fly ash and asphalt with subgrade soils to improve strength and deformation characteristics and reduce swelling and frost heave. Mechanical stabilization - a compacted gravel or granular layer with non-biodegradable reinforcements over soft wet subgrades. Full encapsulation - completely surrounding the soil with geomembranes; partial encapsulation - geomembranes placed horizontally, vertically or both as barriers. Geogrid, geotextile, geonet, geocell, geocomposite and geomembrane are defined. Fines content - percentage finer than the No. 200 sieve. Prefabricated geocomposite edgedrain (PGED) - extruded plastic core with a geotextile filter. Open-graded aggregate base (OGAB), RAP, RCP, RCM, soil cement, subgrade, subbase, unbound base and vacuum preloading are also defined; freeze/thaw requires a frost-susceptible soil, freezing temperatures and water.
key_points: CBR test uses a 3 square inch piston penetrating at 0.05 in./min (p. 9-16).
Freeze/thaw needs frost-susceptible soil, freezing temperatures and available water (p. 9-18).
Layer directly below a PCC slab is now called a base layer, not a subbase (p. 9-21).

sections.title: Mechanical Stabilization: Thicker Granular Layers and Blending
sections.summary: Thick granular layers and blending as mechanical stabilization: benefits of increased load-bearing capacity, frost protection and improved drainage through improved foundation strength, deformation and drainage characteristics.
sections.body: Thick granular layers provide increased load-bearing capacity, frost protection and improved drainage (p. 9-24). The layer may take many forms (stabilized and unstabilized dense graded gravel, open graded gravel, lightweight materials, recycled granular materials), but the strategy in each case is to achieve the desired pavement performance through improved foundation strength, deformation and drainage. The section covers the benefits, typical characteristics and design and construction considerations of granular pavement support.
sections.applicability: Granular working platforms and blended subgrades for pavements over weak soils.

sections.title: Feasibility Considerations
sections.summary: Factors that set the zone to be improved by granular layers: depth, strength and modulus of soft soil, traffic, network importance, constructability, drainage and water table; remove and replace usually preferred for thin zones.
sections.body: The zone selected for improvement depends on the depth of soft soil, its strength and modulus, anticipated traffic loads, importance of the transportation network, constructability, drainage of the geometric design and underlying soil, and depth to water table (p. 9-24). When only a thin zone or short length needs improvement, removal and replacement is usually preferred unless suitable replacement soil is not economically available; 'thin' is intentionally qualitative, set by earthwork economics and the depth of influence of vehicle loads.
key_points: Removal and replacement is usually preferred for a thin zone or short roadway length (p. 9-24).
sections.applicability: Deciding whether a granular layer or blending is feasible for a site.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Applications of thick granular layers (fills, improved subgrade, select borrow, subbase) and frost protection practice of 3 ft or more of gravel; blending of poorly graded in situ soils with other gradations.
sections.body: Thick granular layers, in addition to the design base/subbase, placed over the soft soil or in a partial or full depth excavation, are referred to as fills or embankments, improved or prepared subgrade, and select or preferred borrow, and occasionally used as the subbase (p. 9-24). For frost, a common practice in several states is to use 3 feet or more of gravel beneath the pavement, which improves drainage and gives a weighting action that reduces heave and makes it more uniform; an 18 inch layer of cap rock beneath the pavement has been used successfully by one state in severe frost regions (Ulmeyer et al. 2002). Blending in situ soil with material of different gradation may improve support where compacted soil does not quite meet requirements and is too coarse, too fine or gap-graded (p. 9-25); care is needed to avoid new consequences such as different freeze-thaw behavior. Where blend material must be imported, chemical stabilization of silts and clays will usually be cheaper than importing coarse material, while nearby fine fill to improve coarse or gap-graded material may be cheaper than chemical stabilization.
key_points: A common practice in several states is 3 ft or more of gravel beneath the pavement for frost (p. 9-24).
An 18 inch cap rock layer has been used in severe frost regions (Ulmeyer et al. 2002).
Chemical stabilization of silts and clays is usually cheaper than importing coarse blend material (p. 9-25).
sections.applicability: Granular layers for support and frost protection, and blending of poorly graded subgrades.

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Advantages of thick granular layers (support, uniformity, drainage, frost protection, reduced rutting and pumping) and disadvantages (aggregate cost, loss of gravel into very soft soil when the dumped pile exceeds h > 3c/gamma, excavation and disposal).
sections.body: Where good quality aggregate is readily accessible a thick granular layer may be used; many agencies recognize that weak, poorly draining soils are properly addressed by foundation improvement rather than thicker pavement layers (p. 9-25). Advantages (2.1.2.1): increase supporting capacity of weak fine-grained subgrades; provide a minimum bearing capacity; uniform support over variable soils; reduce seasonal moisture and temperature effects; promote surface runoff; improve subsurface drainage if free draining layers are used; raise pavements in high water table areas; frost protection; reduce subgrade rutting of flexible pavements; reduce pumping and erosion beneath PCC; meet geometric elevation requirements (pp. 9-25 to 9-26). Potential disadvantages (2.1.2.2): expensive where good aggregate is not available; poor aggregate gives inadequate support, drainage, deterioration and frost susceptibility; on extremely soft soils much gravel may be lost by penetration and intrusion, likely when the dumped pile exceeds a height h > (3c/gamma), c the cohesive strength of the subgrade and gamma the unit weight of the granular layer; over excavation as thick as the gravel layer may be required, with disposal costs; the layer gives a working platform but does not strengthen the subgrade, and installation can disturb it (p. 9-26).
key_points: Aggregate loss into a very soft subgrade is likely when the dumped pile height h > 3c/gamma (p. 9-26).
Thick granular layers give a working platform but do not strengthen the subgrade beneath.
Over excavation may be as thick as the gravel layer, and disposal must be included in the cost.
sections.applicability: Weighing granular layer stabilization against other methods.

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Geotechnical, environmental and site feasibility checks for thick gravel and blending: soft soil sensitivity, strength and depth; blending candidates with PI > 12 and R-value < 20; frost susceptibility, disposal, dust, clearing and water levels.
sections.body: Geotechnical (2.1.3.1): sensitivity, strength and depth of the soft subgrade are the key parameters, along with the purpose of the gravel (soft clays, expansive clays or frost heave) and, for deep deposits, consolidation; removal and replacement should always be considered for high organic soils such as peat (p. 9-26). To consider blending, candidate soils typically have a plasticity index greater than 12, a Stabilometer R-value (AASHTO T 190 or ASTM D2844) less than 20, and/or an equivalent DCP (ASTM D6951) number; GW, GP and SW (and potentially GM, GC, SP) soils will most likely need only standard preparation (rip and recompact). For high moisture only, check drainage and consider blending to dry the soil; for gradation problems (GP, GC, SP) blending may be considered; thicker gravel or blending should be considered for high sulfate soils unsuited to chemical stabilization (p. 9-27). Environmental (2.1.3.2): frost susceptibility below the gravel and frost penetration set the layer depth; blending is usually not good where frost is an issue; excavated material may be contaminated or organic; dust control. Site conditions (2.1.3.3): clearing and grubbing and excavation can disturb the subgrade; determine subgrade type, strength/stiffness and sensitivity and groundwater or perched water levels; drainage may be critical.
key_points: Blending candidates: plasticity index greater than 12, R-value less than 20, and/or an equivalent DCP number (p. 9-26).
Remove and replace should always be considered for high organic (peat type) subgrades.
Thicker gravel or blending should be considered for high sulfate soils (p. 9-27).
Blending is usually not a good choice where frost susceptibility is an issue.
sections.applicability: Screening a site for thick gravel or blending stabilization.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: Limitations of thick granular layers and blending: availability of good aggregate, disposal of excavated subgrade, soft ground equipment, sensitive soils, and bearing failure in deep deposits of CBR < 1 soils.
sections.body: The primary limitations are the availability of readily accessible good quality aggregates and the ability to dispose of over excavated subgrade (p. 9-27). Another may be the availability of soft ground construction equipment to over excavate and place gravel without significant disturbance; in sensitive soils disturbance can lead to significant over use of gravel. In deep deposits of extremely soft (CBR < 1) soils the soil may not support equipment or even placement of the gravel without bearing failure.
key_points: In deep deposits of extremely soft soil (CBR < 1) the subgrade may fail in bearing under gravel placement (p. 9-27).
sections.applicability: Recognizing where granular layer stabilization will not work.

sections.title: Alternative Solutions (or Technologies)
sections.summary: Alternatives and complements to thick granular layers: all other stabilization technologies, especially dewatering and geosynthetics which significantly reduce the aggregate thickness required.
sections.body: All of the other stabilization technologies in the chapter should be considered (p. 9-28). Complementary technologies include dewatering and the use of geosynthetics with the aggregate, either or both of which significantly reduce the aggregate thickness needed to stabilize the subgrade and improve long-term performance.
sections.applicability: Identifying complementary methods to reduce gravel thickness.

sections.title: Construction and Materials
sections.summary: Construction and materials for thick granular stabilization layers: soft ground equipment and compaction, and the granular material properties and thicknesses used.
sections.body: This section covers the construction of thick granular stabilization layers (2.2.1) and the materials used for them (2.2.2) (p. 9-28).
sections.applicability: Building granular stabilization layers.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Construction of thick granular layers: low ground pressure equipment to avoid subgrade disturbance, a limit of a few inches of rutting, and adequate compaction of stabilization gravel, subbase and base.
sections.body: Soft ground construction equipment (low ground pressure wide track dozers, extended backhoe grade-all excavators, partially loaded dump trucks) should be considered for over excavation and gravel placement to avoid disturbing the subgrade (p. 9-28). In sensitive soils disturbance can lead to significant over use of gravel or a poorly performing section. Equipment causing subgrade or granular layer rutting of more than a few inches should not be allowed. Adequate compaction of the stabilization gravel, subbase and base must be achieved (see Holtz 1990).
key_points: Equipment that ruts the subgrade or granular layer more than a few inches should not be allowed on site (p. 9-28).
sections.applicability: Placing stabilization gravel over soft subgrades.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Granular materials for stabilization: CBR 20% or greater (about 17,500 psi resilient modulus), A-1 and A-2 soils, dense graded with fines under 5% for seepage, cobbles up to half the lift, and thicknesses of 6 to 12 in. or 1.5 to 5 ft.
sections.body: The two most important characteristics are material properties and thickness (p. 9-28). Strength and stiffness are characterized by CBR, resilient modulus and field plate load tests of the composite. In general materials with CBR of 20% or greater are used, corresponding to resilient moduli of approximately 17,500 psi: sand and/or gravel with limited fines, AASHTO A-1 and A-2 (USCS GW, GP, SW and SP). Sizes up to 4 inches may be used if blended to a well graded material or over a separation layer. Stabilization layers are typically dense-graded; very thick layers may have a bottom lift with cobbles or aggregate of 4 to 8 inches, but no greater than half the lift thickness (pp. 9-28 to 9-29); layers near the roadbed surface follow subbase gradations. Marginal seepage can be achieved by limiting fines to non-plastic material with a fines content less than 5%. Crushed stone has higher shear strength than rounded gravel but may not be economical. Layers 6 to 12 inches thick give uniform support or a construction platform; increasing the composite subgrade design value usually needs a minimum of 1.5 to 5 feet; frost protection fills also range from 1.5 to 5 feet; thicknesses greater than 6 feet have diminishing effects (p. 9-29).
key_points: Granular materials with CBR of 20% or greater (resilient modulus about 17,500 psi) are generally used (p. 9-28).
Bottom lift cobbles of 4 to 8 inches, but no greater than half the lift thickness (p. 9-29).
Fines limited to non-plastic and less than 5% for marginal seepage.
6 to 12 in. for uniformity or a platform; 1.5 to 5 ft to raise the composite subgrade value or for frost; more than 6 ft has diminishing effect.
sections.applicability: Specifying gradation, strength and thickness of granular stabilization layers.

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.summary: Design overview for thick granular layers and blending: composite subgrade design value, gravel thickness methods and blending formulas. Subsections cover: Design Considerations; Design Steps; Primary Design References.
sections.body: This section covers design considerations for a non-homogeneous subgrade (2.3.1), design steps for gravel thickness and blending (2.3.2) and primary design references (2.3.3) (p. 9-29).
sections.applicability: Designing thick granular stabilization layers and blends.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Selecting a single subgrade design value for a non-homogeneous granular-over-soft-soil subgrade: composite reaction between the two extremes, verification by plate load, FWD or LFWD, and caution for layers under 3 ft.
sections.body: A substantial granular layer over weak soil forms a non-homogeneous subgrade, while pavement design needs a single subgrade design value (CBR, resilient modulus or k-value) (p. 9-29). The composite reaction lies between the natural soil and the granular layer, depending on their relative moduli and the layer thickness, and is not known until the layer is placed; it may change once upper layers are placed (confinement, contamination). Characterize individual materials by resilient modulus or CBR and compare with field tests on the constructed embankment and the completed pavement; elastic layer programs can predict the composite response, verified by field testing; agencies use plate load tests, FWD and LFWD (Vennapusa and White 2009) (p. 9-30). Experience shows a good granular layer must be 3 feet or more before the composite reaction resembles that of the granular layer; for layers up to 3 feet the composite modulus can be much less than that of the layer; too high a design value under-designs the pavement; layers less than 1.5 feet thick have minimal impact on the composite reaction under the completed pavement.
key_points: A granular layer must be about 3 ft or more before the composite subgrade reaction resembles that of the granular layer (p. 9-30).
Granular layers less than 1.5 ft thick have minimal impact on the composite subgrade reaction.
Verify the composite subgrade modulus by plate load, FWD or LFWD testing.
sections.applicability: Choosing a design subgrade value where granular fill overlies weak soil.

sections.title: Design Steps
sections.summary: Design steps for thick granular layers: gravel thickness by aggregate surfaced road and haul road methods, and blending of soils to a target gradation.
sections.body: Design steps are given for gravel thickness (2.3.2.1) and for blending (2.3.2.2) (pp. 9-30 to 9-35).
sections.applicability: Following the design procedures for gravel thickness and blending.

sections.title: Gravel Thickness
sections.summary: Gravel stabilization lift thickness by the USFS rut depth equation (Eq. 9-1) with reliability factors (Table 9-5) and by the USFS/FHWA chart method (Figure 9-1) with bearing capacity factors Nc of 2.8, 3.0 and 3.3, plus aggregate filtration checks (Eqs. 9-2, 9-3).
sections.body: The lift can be designed as an unpaved road per AASHTO (1993) or by haul road methods of the USFS (USDA 1977, 1996) or USACE (Barber et al. 1978) (p. 9-30). Rutting is the primary distress; a 2-inch rut in a 4-inch aggregate layer will probably mix subgrade into the aggregate, and ruts over 2 to 3 inches significantly reduce speeds. The USFS (USDA 1996) relates rut depth to CBR (Eq. 9-1, based on the USACE algorithm of Barber et al. 1978), with reliability factors Fr of 1.00, 1.44 and 2.32 for 50, 70 and 90% reliability (Table 9-5, p. 9-31). ESAL factors for a 34-kip tandem axle range from 0.09 to 2.15 for tire pressures of 25 to 100 psi (USDA 1996), versus 1.05 to 1.1 (flexible, SN 1 to 6) and 1.8 to 2 (rigid, D 6 to 14 in.) in AASHTO (1993); reducing tire pressure from 100 to 25 psi can cut rut depth by more than 50%. Skorseth and Selim (2000) give catalog and analytical approaches (p. 9-32). The USFS chart method (USDA 1977) applies to high quality cohesionless fill (lab CBR per ASTM D1883 >= 80), fewer than 10,000 passes and subgrade undrained strength less than about 2000 psf (CBR < 3). Steps: (1) identify subgrade CBR, groundwater, AASHTO/USCS class and sensitivity; (2) determine thickness t for a construction platform from Figure 9-1 (single or dual wheel, 80 psi), selecting Nc = 2.8 for low ruts (< 2 in.), 3.0 for moderate (2 to 4 in.), 3.3 for large (> 4 in.), or local charts, and select the greater t (p. 9-34); (3) check filtration of the gravel (Eqs. 9-2 and 9-3).
key_points: Table 9-5 (p. 9-31): Fr = 1.00 at 50%, 1.44 at 70%, 2.32 at 90% reliability.
Chart method limits: fill CBR >= 80 and nonplastic, fewer than 10,000 passes, subgrade CBR < 3 (p. 9-32).
Nc without geosynthetic: 2.8 (< 2 in. ruts), 3.0 (2 to 4 in.), 3.3 (> 4 in.) (p. 9-34).
Reducing tire pressure on a 34-kip tandem from 100 to 25 psi can reduce ruts by more than 50% (p. 9-31).
equations: Eq. 9-1: Rut Depth (inches) = 5.833 (Fr R)^0.2476 / [ (log t)^0.02 C1^0.9335 C2^0.2848 ]; USFS rut depth for aggregate surfaced roads, R = ESALs at 80 psi, t = top layer thickness (in.), C1 = CBR of top layer, C2 = CBR of subgrade, Fr = reliability factor
Eq. 9-2: D15 of aggregate < 5 x D85 of subgrade; filtration (retention) check for stabilization gravel
Eq. 9-3: D15 of aggregate > 5 x D15 of subgrade; filtration (permeability) check for stabilization gravel
figures: Figure 9-1: Stabilization aggregate thickness design curves for a single wheel load (top) and dual wheel loads (bottom).
tables: Table 9-5: Reliability Factors for use in Equation 9-1

sections.title: Blending
sections.summary: Blending soils to a target gradation: the power-law size distribution P = 100(d/D)^n with maximum density near n = 0.5 (Eq. 9-4) and the combined percent passing P = Aa + Bb + Cc ... (Eq. 9-5), by analytical or graphical trial methods.
sections.body: Soil mixing can alter particle properties for better stability or drainage; aggregate gradation is expressed by Eq. 9-4 (Barksdale 1991, Krebs and Walker 1971, Rollings and Rollings 1996) (p. 9-34). Maximum density may be achieved when n = 0.5; higher density helps frictional strength; grading for maximum density depends on angularity, shape, surface roughness, size and construction method, and the amount and plasticity of fines govern behavior (p. 9-35). Analytical and graphical procedures are in Krebs and Walker (1971), Barksdale (1991), Rollings and Rollings (1996) and Jones et al. (2010); spreadsheets and programs also exist. Blending two or more soils to a specification uses Eq. 9-5 for the combined percent passing a sieve, by trial combinations. The graphical method is straightforward but complicated for more than two soils; the analytical method is more precise and extends to more than two soils; blending precision is usually limited by field conditions.
key_points: Maximum density may be achieved when n = 0.5 in Eq. 9-4 (p. 9-34).
The analytical method extends easily to more than two soils; field conditions usually limit blending precision (p. 9-35).
equations: Eq. 9-4: P = 100 (d/D)^n; percent finer P for sieve size d, maximum particle size D, coefficient n
Eq. 9-5: P = A x a + B x b + C x c + ...; percent of combined aggregate passing a sieve, A, B, C = percent of each aggregate passing, a, b, c = proportions
sections.applicability: Proportioning blended soils to a target gradation.

sections.title: Primary Design References
sections.summary: Primary design references for thick gravel (AASHTO 1993, Barber et al. 1978, Skorseth and Selim 2000, USDA 1977 and 1996) and for blending (Barksdale 1991, Jones et al. 2010, Krebs and Walker 1971, Rollings and Rollings 1996).
sections.body: Thick gravel (2.3.3.1): AASHTO (1993); Barber, Odom and Patrich (1978), The Deterioration and Reliability of Pavements; Skorseth and Selim (2000), Gravel Road Maintenance and Design Manual; USDA (1977), Guidelines for Use of Fabrics in Construction and Maintenance of Low-Volume Roads; USDA (1996), Earth and Aggregate Surfacing Design Guide for Low Volume Roads (pp. 9-35 to 9-36). Blending (2.3.3.2): Barksdale (1991), The Aggregate Handbook; Jones et al. (2010); Krebs and Walker (1971), Highway Materials; Rollings and Rollings (1996).

sections.title: Overview of Construction Specifications and Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Specifications and quality assurance for thick granular stabilization layers: gradation, compacted CBR, durability and thickness, and quality control and monitoring.
sections.body: This section covers specification development (2.4.1), quality assurance (2.4.2) and instrumentation monitoring and construction control (2.4.3) for thick granular layers (p. 9-36).
sections.applicability: Specifying and checking granular stabilization layers.

sections.title: Specification Development
sections.summary: Specifying stabilization gravel: gradation, compacted CBR at specified moisture-density, durability and thickness, with design charts based on a minimum gravel CBR of 80 and maximum rut depth as a performance measure.
sections.body: Specifications of gradation, compacted CBR of the gravel for specific moisture-density requirements, durability and thickness are required (p. 9-36). Gravel thickness is based on subgrade CBR and the design charts assume a minimum CBR = 80 for the gravel. Gradation is critical to provide separation from the subgrade. Maximum rut depth should be included as a performance measure. Aggregate at or near the site should be tested for suitability and thickness; for hauled materials agency aggregate specifications are strongly recommended, as quarries stock them at lower cost than special gradations.
key_points: Design charts assume a minimum gravel CBR = 80 (p. 9-36).
Include maximum rut depth as a performance measure in the specification.
sections.applicability: Writing specifications for stabilization gravel.

sections.title: Summary of Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Quality control of granular stabilization layers: moisture, density or stiffness and thickness, GPS thickness control with point checks, DCP testing of strength and effective depth, and proof rolling.
sections.body: Primary quality control considerations are moisture, density or stiffness, and thickness (p. 9-37). Modern GPS can control thickness, with point checks for reliability. The DCP test can determine strength and effective depth of the in-place aggregate. Proof rolling should be performed to evaluate deformation and rutting potential.
sections.applicability: Quality control during placement of stabilization gravel.

sections.title: Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control
sections.summary: Monitoring granular stabilization: rut depth measurement, instrumented proofrolling, intelligent compaction mapping, and FWD or LFWD to determine an equivalent subgrade stiffness for design.
sections.body: Monitoring typically consists of measuring rut depth against design requirements (p. 9-37). Proofrolling can be instrumented to monitor deformation and rutting. Intelligent compaction can map areas needing improvement, confirm uniformity and indicate the composite stiffness achieved (see GeoTechTools). If the aggregate is incorporated in the pavement design, FWD or LFWD tests can determine the equivalent subgrade stiffness, provided gradation prevents long-term degradation.
sections.applicability: Monitoring and verifying granular stabilization layers.

sections.title: Cost Data
sections.summary: Cost data for thick granular stabilization layers: cost components of thick granular layers: granular material and excavation and disposal by the ton, typical gravel cost of $7 to $20/ton, and extra cost for light construction equipment.
sections.body: This section gives the cost components for thick granular layers and blending (p. 9-37).
sections.applicability: Estimating the cost of granular stabilization.

sections.title: Cost Components
sections.summary: Cost components of thick granular layers: granular material and excavation and disposal by the ton, typical gravel cost of $7 to $20/ton, and extra cost for light construction equipment.
sections.body: Costs include the granular material (by the ton) and excavation and disposal (also by the ton) (p. 9-37). Granular material typically ranges from $7 to $20/ton, influenced by specifications and haul distance and conditions. Equipment is common to highway projects so added mobilization is negligible, but extras may arise if light equipment (wide track low ground pressure dozers, grade-all excavators, partially loaded dump trucks, scrapers) is required because of effects on construction rates. See GeoTechTools for a conceptual cost estimating tool.
key_points: Granular material typically costs $7 to $20/ton (p. 9-37).
sections.applicability: Pricing gravel stabilization layers.

sections.title: Mechanical Stabilization: Geosynthetics
sections.summary: Geosynthetic mechanical stabilization of pavement subgrades: geogrids and geotextiles with a granular layer give lateral restraint, bearing capacity increase and membrane support, plus separation, filtration and drainage.
sections.body: Section 3.0 (pp. 9-38 to 9-63) covers geosynthetics used with granular layers for subgrade separation and stabilization: feasibility, construction and materials, design (Tables 9-6 to 9-8, Figures 9-5 and 9-6), specifications and quality assurance, and cost.
sections.applicability: Using geosynthetics with aggregate to stabilize soft or fine-grained pavement subgrades.

sections.title: Feasibility Considerations
sections.summary: How geosynthetics stabilize: lateral restraint of aggregate, increased bearing capacity, separation, filtration and in-plane drainage; AASHTO M 288 stabilization for undrained strength below about 2000 psf (CBR about 3) and separation for CBR >= 3.
sections.body: Geosynthetics can be used most anyplace more gravel would be used and allow gravel on much weaker soil (p. 9-38). Placed on weak, often saturated subgrades with a granular layer, they stabilize the subgrade and give a working platform for unpaved roads, flexible and rigid pavements. Soft subgrades give little lateral restraint; a geogrid with good interlock or a geotextile with good friction gives tensile resistance to lateral aggregate movement, increasing horizontal stress and reducing rutting, and forces the bearing surface along a longer path, increasing system bearing capacity. The geosynthetic must also separate: only a small amount of fines in the granular layer reduces shear strength, modulus and permeability and increases frost susceptibility. Geogrids do not prevent intrusion of subgrade soils, so a geotextile is needed with open graded gravel that does not meet filtration/separation requirements. It must also filter, allowing excess pore pressure to dissipate, which also allows subgrade strength gain (p. 9-39); needle-punched nonwovens or drainage geocomposites give in-plane drainage. AASHTO M 288 identifies mechanical stabilization as most applicable where undrained shear strength is less than about 2000 psf (CBR about 3); some rutting will occur after a few hundred passes (Webster 1993). For CBR >= 3 soils that are seasonally weak or pumping-susceptible, the application is separation.
key_points: Reinforcement, separation, filtration and drainage combine to give mechanical stabilization (FHWA 2008) (p. 9-39).
Only a small amount of fines in the granular layer reduces its shear strength, modulus and permeability (p. 9-38).
Use a geotextile with a geogrid if the aggregate does not meet filtration/separation requirements.
AASHTO M 288: stabilization for su < about 2000 psf (CBR about 3); separation for CBR >= 3 (p. 9-39).
sections.applicability: Deciding whether a geosynthetic stabilization or separation layer suits a subgrade.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Applications of geosynthetics with aggregate: stabilization for CBR < 3, stabilization layer for marginal CBR about 3 to 4, separation up to CBR = 8, lateral restraint, bearing support and membrane support for ruts over about 4 in.
sections.body: Where soft subgrades are present (CBR < 3) geosynthetics reduce stabilization gravel and enhance subgrade improvement; for marginal subgrades (CBR about 3 to 4) they are placed between base or subbase and subgrade as a stabilization layer; as separation they serve subgrades with fines up to CBR = 8, especially with open graded gravel (p. 9-39). Separation (3.1.1.1): geotextiles over high fines subgrades prevent fines migration into stabilization, base or subbase layers, maintaining effective thickness and drainage and improving reliability and roadway life (p. 9-40). Stabilization (3.1.1.2): primarily to facilitate construction; lateral restraint reduces rutting or aggregate thickness (Figure 9-2, top); reinforcement prevents localized bearing failure (middle); if ruts exceed about 4 inches the geosynthetic is tensioned and gives membrane support (bottom); the stabilized layer helps contractors meet compaction for the first two or three lifts. Long-term, the geosynthetic maintains the section and base integrity and gives improved support during overload or seasonally weak conditions (pp. 9-41 to 9-42).
key_points: Stabilization for CBR < 3; stabilization layer for CBR about 3 to 4; separation for subgrades with fines up to CBR = 8 (p. 9-39).
Membrane support develops when ruts exceed about 4 in. (p. 9-40).
figures: Figure 9-2: Possible reinforcement functions provided by geosynthetics in roadways: lateral restraint (top), bearing capacity increase (middle), and membrane tension support (bottom).
sections.applicability: Matching separation or stabilization geosynthetics to subgrade strength.

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Benefits of geosynthetic separation (CBR 3 to 8) and stabilization (CBR < 3 to 4): less aggregate and excavation, lower subgrade stress and disturbance, strength gain, uniform support; drawbacks are cost assessment, product selection and installation care.
sections.body: Advantages (3.1.2.1): separators on firm subgrades (CBR 3 to 8) with high fines prevent aggregate penetration and fines pumping and may allow open-graded free draining aggregates (p. 9-42). Stabilization of soft to marginal subgrades (CBR < 3 to 4) can also reduce aggregate thickness, reduce excavation of unsuitable soil, reduce stress intensity on the subgrade, reduce construction disturbance, increase soft subgrade strength over time, and give more uniform support over variable subgrades and cut-fill transitions (consolidation settlements are not reduced by geosynthetic reinforcement). Both can reduce maintenance and extend pavement life. Potential disadvantages (3.1.2.2): a long-term cost benefit assessment is needed for some applications (the geosynthetic is often paid for by aggregate savings but may increase cost); products work well under some conditions and not others, so lab performance tests or test sections may be needed; special storage, handling, placement and compaction procedures are needed to prevent damage (p. 9-43).
key_points: Consolidation settlements are not reduced by geosynthetic reinforcement (p. 9-42).
Lab performance tests or test sections may be needed to choose a geosynthetic (p. 9-43).
sections.applicability: Weighing geosynthetic stabilization for a roadway project.

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Subgrade conditions optimum for geosynthetic stabilization: SC, CL, CH, ML, MH, OL, OH, PT soils, cu < 2000 psf or soaked CBR < 3, R-value < 20, MR < 4500 psi, high water table and high sensitivity; fines migration seen up to CBR 8.
sections.body: Geotechnical (3.1.3.1): the considerations for thicker gravel also apply; based on 40 years of experience the optimum subgrade conditions for geosynthetics are poor soils (USCS SC, CL, CH, ML, MH, OL, OH, PT; AASHTO A-5, A-6, A-7-5, A-7-6), low undrained shear strength (cu < 2000 psf, CBR < 3 as soaked saturated CBR per ASTM D4429; R-value about < 20, MR about < 4500 psi), high water table and high sensitivity (p. 9-43). Significant fines migration has been observed at subgrade CBR as high as 8 (Al-Qadi et al. 1998). Environmental (3.1.3.2): frost susceptibility and penetration may require a greater thickness than stabilization; excavated material must be evaluated for contamination; dust control if the aggregate has fines (p. 9-44). Site conditions (3.1.3.3): clearing and grubbing, water table and drainage, subgrade type, strength, stiffness and sensitivity; geosynthetics give better control of subgrade disturbance; consider on-site disposal and, for deep soft deposits, consolidation and its effect on adjacent facilities.
key_points: Optimum for geosynthetics: cu < 2000 psf, soaked CBR < 3, R-value < about 20, MR < about 4500 psi (p. 9-43).
Fines migration observed with subgrade CBR as high as 8 (Al-Qadi et al. 1998).
Frost thickness requirements may exceed stabilization requirements (p. 9-44).
sections.applicability: Screening a subgrade for geosynthetic stabilization.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: Limitations of geosynthetic stabilization: no standardized method to compare products, test sections recommended, geocomposites usually best at higher cost, installation damage, and limited life cycle cost data.
sections.body: One problem is the absence of a standardized method to evaluate differences between geosynthetic products; mechanistic-empirical design may solve this, but test or demonstration sections are recommended meanwhile (e.g., AASHTO 2014b) (p. 9-44). Geogrids and geotextiles each work well in some conditions and one may outperform the other in others; geocomposites (e.g., geotextile/geogrid) tend to work best in most stabilization applications at greater material cost. Care is needed during installation to prevent damage. Geosynthetics have been used on thousands of projects for over 40 years with promising long-term data, but more life cycle cost benefit data is needed.
key_points: Geocomposites tend to work best in most stabilization applications, at greater material cost (p. 9-44).
sections.applicability: Recognizing limits on geosynthetic product selection.

sections.title: Construction and Materials
sections.summary: Construction steps and material properties for geosynthetic stabilization layers: four construction steps for geosynthetic stabilization: prepare ground with little or no rutting (< 2 in.), unroll without dragging with at least 12 in. overlaps, end dump and spread fill (adjust if ruts exceed 3 in.), and exhume a section to check damage, patching 18 in. beyond.
sections.body: This section covers construction of geosynthetic stabilization layers (3.2.1) and the geotextile, geogrid and geocomposite materials (3.2.2) (p. 9-45).
sections.applicability: Installing geosynthetic stabilization layers.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Four construction steps for geosynthetic stabilization: prepare ground with little or no rutting (< 2 in.), unroll without dragging with at least 12 in. overlaps, end dump and spread fill (adjust if ruts exceed 3 in.), and exhume a section to check damage, patching 18 in. beyond.
sections.body: Guidance is in AASHTO (2014a) and FHWA (2008) (p. 9-45). Step 1, ground preparation: undercut as required; minimize disturbance, allowing only equipment giving little (less than 2 inches) or no ruts. Step 2, rolling out: do not drag the geosynthetic; place it flat and taut with no wrinkles (staples or pins may hold it); check and repair or replace damage; overlap adjacent rolls at least 12 inches (or per specification) unless sewn, with the upper sheet in the direction of fill placement; sewn seams stitches up; no equipment on the geosynthetic until covered with the minimum lift. Step 3, fill: end dump onto previously placed aggregate, spread and grade; if rutting exceeds 3 inches increase lift thickness or reduce vehicle weight; no vibratory compaction on the first lift over very soft ground; fill ruts, never blade them down (p. 9-46). Step 4: remove fill in one small section to check damage; if damaged modify placement and repair with a replacement or a patch extending at least 18 inches outside the damaged area. The steps are illustrated in Figures 9-3 and 9-4.
key_points: Overlap adjacent geosynthetics at least 12 in. unless sewn (p. 9-45).
If ruts exceed 3 in., increase lift thickness or decrease vehicle weight.
No vibratory compaction on the first lift over very soft ground (p. 9-46).
Patches extend at least 18 in. beyond damage.
figures: Figure 9-3: Installation of geosynthetics in soil stabilization: prepare the ground (upper left), unroll geosynthetic (upper right), back dump aggregate (middle left), spread aggregate (middle left), and compact aggregate (bottom).
Figure 9-4: Fill in ruts – do not blade down.
sections.applicability: Field installation of geotextiles and geogrids under stabilization aggregate.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Geosynthetic material properties for stabilization: survivability-controlled strength (High, Moderate, Low; Types 1 to 3), opening and permittivity requirements, elongation, AOS, UV stability, durability (avoid polyester above pH 9), geogrid apertures and geocomposite bonding.
sections.body: Required properties are those to perform the primary and secondary functions over the system life and those to survive installation (p. 9-47). Separation and filtration relate to opening characteristics and the gradation of adjacent layers. Construction stresses can far exceed in-service stresses, so strength is usually governed by survivability. FHWA (2008) and AASHTO (2014a) tables relate index properties (grab, CBR puncture and tear strength for geotextiles; wide width and junction strength for geogrids) to survivability classes High (Type 1), Moderate (Type 2) and Low (Type 3). Berg et al. (2000) recommended reporting 2% and 5% secant moduli, pullout and direct shear coefficients, aperture size and percent open area in future studies (p. 9-48). Geotextiles (3.2.2.1): elongation at break is typically < 50% for wovens and > 50% for nonwovens, so strength requirements are greater for wovens; AOS is essentially the largest opening; permittivity measures flow; UV stability needed; durability life should be well in excess of 1000 yrs; use polypropylene rather than polyester for pH > 9 (lime or cement). Geogrids (3.2.2.2): extruded, woven (coated) or welded; strength by wide width and junction strength; apertures sized for interlock (too small, gravel slides; too large, less confinement); less UV-susceptible; use polypropylene or polyethylene for pH > 9 (p. 9-49). Geocomposites (3.2.2.3): woven/nonwoven, geotextile/geogrid, nonwoven with high modulus filaments, geotextile/geonet; bonding must hold; sliding of one component over another reduces performance (Christopher and Schwartz 2010).
key_points: For subgrade stabilization, geosynthetic survivability tends to control the strength requirements (p. 9-47).
Woven geotextiles typically < 50% elongation at break, nonwovens > 50%; strength requirements are greater for wovens (p. 9-48).
Use polypropylene (or polyethylene for geogrids) rather than polyester where pH > 9.
Geogrid apertures too small let gravel slide; too large reduce interlock (p. 9-49).
sections.applicability: Selecting geotextile, geogrid or geocomposite properties for stabilization.

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.summary: Design overview for geosynthetic separation and stabilization: design-by-function with AASHTO M 288, the FHWA (2008) steps, and the Caltrans selection flow chart.
sections.body: This section covers design considerations (3.3.1), design steps for separation and stabilization (3.3.2) and primary design references (3.3.3) (p. 9-50).
sections.applicability: Designing geosynthetic separation and stabilization layers.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Design considerations for separation and stabilization geosynthetics: filtration compatibility, survivability and endurance, design by function with AASHTO M 288, the Caltrans (2014) selection chart, and a composite support equivalent to CBR = 3 (MR 4500 psi).
sections.body: A separator geotextile must prevent intermixing of the permeable base and the subgrade or subbase, satisfy filtration criteria for the subgrade gradation and permeability, and satisfy survivability and endurance criteria (FHWA 2008) (p. 9-50). For stabilization the geosynthetic must also separate, filter wet, often saturated subgrades and reinforce, with stronger survivability criteria; design is by function with AASHTO M 288 following FHWA (2008). The structural pavement design is not modified, but the subgrade support value can be improved. Caltrans (2014) developed the flow chart in Figure 9-5 for selection based on subgrade strength and gradation and the gradation compatibility of the base/subbase (p. 9-52). The pavement is designed as if the geosynthetic were absent; the geosynthetic replaces extra unbound material for construction and no part of the pavement section. If the soil has CBR less than 3 and the aggregate thickness is set by a low rutting criterion, the composite system is theoretically equivalent to CBR = 3 (resilient modulus 4500 psi), to be confirmed by plate load or FWD testing. The FHWA procedure is controlled by soil CBR measured per ASTM D4429.
key_points: Pavement is designed as if the geosynthetic were not present (p. 9-52).
With CBR < 3 subgrade and a low rut design, the composite support is theoretically equivalent to CBR = 3 (MR 4500 psi).
Figure 9-5 Class 1+ geotextiles are stronger than AASHTO Class 1 (p. 9-51).
figures: Figure 9-5: Selecting an appropriate subgrade stabilization geosynthetic.
sections.applicability: Setting up a geosynthetic stabilization design and choosing a product class.

sections.title: Design Steps
sections.summary: Design steps from FHWA (2008) for geosynthetic separation (CBR >= 3) and stabilization (CBR < 3) applications. Subsections cover: Separation; Stabilization.
sections.body: Design steps are given for separation (3.3.2.1) and stabilization (3.3.2.2) applications, after FHWA (2008) (pp. 9-52 to 9-60).
sections.applicability: Following the FHWA design procedures for geosynthetics in roadways.

sections.title: Separation
sections.summary: FHWA (2008) separation design: need for a separator (CBR about 3 to 8, high fines), opening and permittivity per Table 9-6, retention and permeability checks (Eqs. 9-6 to 9-8), Class 2 survivability, and at least 6 in. of base between wheel and geotextile.
sections.body: Step 1: assess need; separators suit high fines subgrades (CL, CH, ML, MH, CM, GM, OL, OH) with CBR about 3 to 8 (MR about 4500 to 12,000 psi, Su about 2000 to 5000 psf, R about 18 to 37) (p. 9-52). Step 2: maximum opening and minimum permittivity from AASHTO M 288 (Table 9-6, p. 9-53): Class 2 grab strength 250 lb (1100 N) for elongation < 50% and 157 lb (700 N) for > 50%; sewn seam 220 (990) and 140 (630); tear 90 (400) and 56 (250); puncture (D6241) 495 (2200) and 309 (1375); UV 50% retained after 500 hours; AOS < 0.6 mm for < 50% passing No. 200 and < 0.3 mm for > 50%; permittivity > 0.02 sec-1 and > that of soil. Values are minimum average roll values in the weaker direction; acceptance per ASTM D4759 and D4354 (p. 9-54). Check AOS, permeability and permittivity with Eqs. 9-6 to 9-8; for noncohesive silts and highly pumping soils use AOS <= D85 and lab filtration tests. Step 3: survivability; use Class 2 for subgrade CBR > 3 with at least 6 inches of base/subbase and normal equipment and for edgedrain filters; Class 1 (Table 9-7) for CBR < 3 and heavy equipment; keep at least 6 inches of base/subbase between wheel and geotextile. Very poor subgrades (R <= 5, CBR about <= 1.5) may warrant stronger than Class 1 (Caltrans 2014) (p. 9-56). Step 4: follow Section 3.2.1.
key_points: Separation applies to high fines subgrades with CBR about 3 to 8 (p. 9-52).
Table 9-6 Class 2: grab 250 lb (< 50% elongation) or 157 lb (> 50%); AOS < 0.6 mm or < 0.3 mm by fines; permittivity > 0.02 sec-1 (p. 9-53).
Keep at least 6 in. of base/subbase between the wheel and the geotextile at all times (p. 9-54).
For noncohesive silts use AOS <= D85 and run laboratory filtration tests.

sections.title: Stabilization
sections.summary: FHWA (2008) stabilization design: design pavement without the geosynthetic, take 50% of extra mixing aggregate t1, construction platform thickness t2 from Figure 9-6 with Nc 5, 5.5, 6 (geotextiles) or 5.8 (geogrid with separator), filtration (Eqs. 9-6 to 9-8) and survivability per Tables 9-7 and 9-8.
sections.body: Steps (FHWA 2008) (p. 9-56): (1) identify subgrade CBR, groundwater, AASHTO/USCS class and sensitivity; (2) compare with Section 3.1.3.1 or local policy to decide if a geosynthetic is needed; (3) design the pavement without the geosynthetic; (4) determine any extra aggregate t1 to ameliorate mixing at the base/subgrade interface and reduce it by 50%; (5) determine the aggregate t2 for a construction platform from Figure 9-6 (the same charts as Section 2.3.2.1), selecting for geotextiles Nc = 5 for low ruts (< 2 in.), 5.5 moderate (2 to 4 in.), 6 large (> 4 in.), and for geogrids with a geotextile separator Nc = 5.8 for low to moderate rutting; Giroud and Han (2004a, 2004b) may also be used for geogrids (p. 9-58); (6) select the greater of t2 or 50% t1; (7) check filtration (Eqs. 9-6 to 9-8), or for geogrids the aggregate per Section 2.3 or a geotextile with the grid; (8) survivability: geotextiles per AASHTO M 288 class (Table 9-7, p. 9-55: Class 1 grab 315 lb (1400 N) / 200 lb (900 N), seam 280 / 180 lb, tear 110 / 80 lb, puncture 620 / 433 lb, AOS < 0.43 mm or < 0.3 mm, permittivity 0.5, 0.2 or 0.1 sec-1 for < 15, 15 to 50, > 50% passing No. 200; woven slit film not allowed) and geogrids per Table 9-8 (p. 9-60: multi-rib tensile 1230 lb/ft (18 kN/m) Class 1, 820 (12) Classes 2 and 3; junction strength 25 lb (110 N) for Classes 1 and 2 and 8 lb (35 N) for Class 3; aperture 0.5 to 3 in. with D50 <= aperture <= 2 D85 of aggregate; separation D15 aggregate < 5 D85 subgrade). Default is Class 1 for stabilization; very poor subgrades (R <= 5, CBR about <= 1.5) may need stronger than Class 1 (p. 9-59).

Nc for geotextiles: 5 (< 2 in. ruts), 5.5 (2 to 4 in.), 6 (> 4 in.); geogrid with separator: 5.8 (p. 9-58).
