sections.title: Primary Design References
sections.summary: Primary design references for geosynthetic stabilization of roadway subgrades: AASHTO R 50 (2014b), FHWA (2008) guidelines, Giroud and Han (2004a, 2004b) geogrid unpaved road method and USDA (1977).
sections.body: References (p. 9-61): AASHTO (2014b) R 50-09(2013), Geosynthetic Reinforcement of the Aggregate Base Course of Flexible Pavement Structures; FHWA (2008), Geosynthetic Design and Construction Guidelines (Holtz, Christopher and Berg); Giroud and Han (2004a, 2004b), design method for geogrid-reinforced unpaved roads, parts I and II, ASCE JGGE 130(8); USDA (1977), Guidelines for Use of Fabrics in Construction and Maintenance of Low-Volume Roads.
sections.applicability: Finding design sources for geosynthetic stabilization.

sections.title: Geosynthetics Overview of Construction Specifications and Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Specifications, quality assurance and monitoring for geosynthetic stabilization layers. Subsections cover: Specification Development; Summary of Quality Assurance; Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control.
sections.body: This section covers specification development (3.4.1), quality assurance (3.4.2) and instrumentation monitoring and construction control (3.4.3) for geosynthetic stabilization layers (p. 9-61).
sections.applicability: Specifying and checking geosynthetic stabilization.

sections.title: Specification Development
sections.summary: Specifications for geosynthetic stabilization layers from AASHTO M 288, AASHTO R 50-09 and FHWA-NHI-07-092 and GeoTechTools: survivability, retention and filtration requirements, seams, sequencing and an engineer's representative on site.
sections.body: Detailed specifications are in AASHTO M 288 (2014a), AASHTO R 50-09 (2014b), FHWA-NHI-07-092 (FHWA 2008) and GeoTechTools; each gives guide specifications to be modified for local conditions and example specifications (p. 9-61). Main considerations are minimum geosynthetic requirements from survivability, retention and filtration (Section 3.3) and construction requirements (Sections 3.2 and 3.3), including seam lap and sewing, construction sequencing and quality control. An engineer's representative should be on site to confirm the correct geosynthetic, the specified sequence and that no damage occurs.
sections.applicability: Writing geosynthetic stabilization specifications.

sections.title: Summary of Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Quality assurance for geosynthetic stabilization: subgrade condition, aggregate placement, lift thickness, equipment, GPS and DCP checks, rut limits, proofrolling, and exhuming about 1 ft2 to inspect for damage.
sections.body: Attention should be paid to factors affecting survivability: subgrade condition, aggregate placement, lift thickness, equipment operations and visual observations (p. 9-62). Primary quality control is moisture, density or stiffness and thickness of aggregate above the geosynthetic; GPS with point checks; DCP for strength and effective depth. Rutting should be limited to tolerable design levels; fill ruts and do not blade them down. Proofroll. After the initial lift, excavate a small section to expose approximately 1 ft2 or more for damage; if damaged, examine more sections, repair by replacement or patch, and increase initial lift thickness and/or use lighter ground pressure equipment.
key_points: Expose approximately 1 ft2 or more of geosynthetic after the first lift to inspect for damage (p. 9-62).
sections.applicability: Field quality checks on geosynthetic stabilization.

sections.title: Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control
sections.summary: Monitoring geosynthetic stabilization: rut depth, FWD or LFWD for an equivalent subgrade resilient modulus, instrumented proofrolling, intelligent compaction, and strain-gaged geosynthetics.
sections.body: Monitoring typically measures rut depth against the geosynthetic and gravel design (p. 9-62). If the stabilization layer is incorporated in the pavement design, FWD or LFWD tests can give an equivalent subgrade stiffness, a valid equivalent subgrade resilient modulus for design given that the geotextile mitigates long-term degradation from intrusion and pumping. Instrumented proofrolling and intelligent compaction confirm uniformity and composite stiffness. The geosynthetic can be instrumented with strain gages offsite to evaluate stress/strain at the subgrade; one product is sold with fiber optic strain gages built in.
sections.applicability: Verifying performance of geosynthetic stabilized subgrades.

sections.title: Geosynthetic Cost Data
sections.summary: Cost data for geosynthetic stabilization: geosynthetic stabilization costs: separation geotextiles about $1.00/yd2 in place, stabilization geotextiles $1 to $2.50/yd2, geogrids $1.50 to $4.00/yd2, gravel $7 to $20/ton, and typical aggregate thickness reduction of 20 to 40%.
sections.body: This section gives the cost components of geosynthetic stabilization (p. 9-63).
sections.applicability: Estimating the cost of geosynthetic stabilization.

sections.title: Cost Components
sections.summary: Geosynthetic stabilization costs: separation geotextiles about $1.00/yd2 in place, stabilization geotextiles $1 to $2.50/yd2, geogrids $1.50 to $4.00/yd2, gravel $7 to $20/ton, and typical aggregate thickness reduction of 20 to 40%.
sections.body: Cost components are the geosynthetic (by the square yard), placement and any additional stabilization aggregate (per ton) (p. 9-63). Equipment is common to highway projects; very soft subgrades may need light equipment, adding cost with or without geosynthetics. In-place cost of separation geotextiles is on the order of $1.00/yd2; for soft soil stabilization $1 to $2.50/yd2 for geotextiles and $1.50 to $4.00/yd2 for geogrids; in-place compacted gravel $7 to $20/ton. Compared with thicker aggregate alone, the geosynthetic typically reduces aggregate thickness by 20 to 40%. Assuming in-place gravel at 120 lb/ft3, a six-inch layer costs on the order of $1.80 to $5.40/yd2, a typical saving for a CBR = 2 subgrade, plus savings from not over-excavating and disposing 6 inches of subgrade and better long-term performance.
key_points: Separation geotextile in place about $1.00/yd2; stabilization geotextiles $1 to $2.50/yd2; geogrids $1.50 to $4.00/yd2 (p. 9-63).
Geosynthetics typically reduce aggregate thickness by 20 to 40%.
A 6 in. gravel layer at 120 lb/ft3 costs about $1.80 to $5.40/yd2.
sections.applicability: Comparing geosynthetic stabilization cost with thicker aggregate.

sections.title: Mechanical Stabilization: Lightweight Fill
sections.summary: Lightweight fill (geofoam, foamed concrete, wood fiber, tire shreds, expanded shale and clay, fly ash, boiler slag, air-cooled slag) as an alternative to aggregate replacement for pavement subgrade stabilization over deep soft deposits.
sections.body: An alternative to replacement with aggregate is lightweight fill, including geofoam, foamed concrete, wood fiber, tire shreds, expanded shale and clay, fly ash, boiler slag, air-cooled slag and others (p. 9-64). They should especially be considered in deeper deposits where shallow surface stabilization may not be effective and thicker aggregate would control deformation under wheel load but increase concerns for settlement and stability. The materials are covered in the Lightweight Fill chapter; this section focuses on their use for stabilization of pavements and refers to that chapter.
sections.applicability: Pavement subgrade stabilization over deep compressible soils where added weight is a concern.

sections.title: Feasibility Considerations
sections.summary: Feasibility of lightweight fill for pavement support: caution with degradable materials such as wood fiber, buoyancy and uplift of very light materials (down to 0.70 lb/ft3) under flooding, anchoring cover, and differential icing over insulating materials.
sections.body: Practically any lightweight fill in Chapter 3 is feasible for improving pavement support, but caution is advised for materials that could degrade over time (e.g., wood fibers), which could harm ride quality and structural integrity (p. 9-64). Materials range from the lower end of soil unit weights down to 0.70 lb/ft3; the lighter end raises concern for buoyancy and uplift of the pavement (Figure 9-7). The design must be checked for uplift where flooding or a rising water table can reach the layer, requiring an anchoring system (e.g., soil fill on top) or other measures (p. 9-65). Insulating materials (e.g., geofoam) raise differential icing concerns in cold regions. The primary issue is the pavement support the materials provide.
key_points: Lightweight fills down to 0.70 lb/ft3 raise buoyancy and uplift concerns (p. 9-64).
Check uplift where flooding or a rising water table can reach the layer; provide an anchoring soil cover (p. 9-65).
figures: Figure 9-7: Uplift due to flooding of pavement section using lightweight fill.
sections.applicability: Screening lightweight fill for pavement stabilization.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Lightweight fill reduces settlement and increases stability for pavements over soft subgrades and deep compressible deposits, giving immediate improvement that can accelerate construction despite higher cost.
sections.body: Lightweight fill can reduce settlement and increase stability for pavements over soft subgrades and should especially be considered for deep compressible deposits (p. 9-65). Although more costly than most other stabilization methods, it gives immediate improvement and accelerates construction; on some projects the time saving may be worth more than the cost difference.
sections.applicability: Pavements over deep compressible soils needing fast construction.

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Advantages of lightweight fill stabilization (faster construction, less settlement and instability, frost mitigation, uniform support) and disadvantages (availability, cost, leachate, durability and differential icing).
sections.body: Advantages (4.1.2.1): accelerated construction with fewer site access problems (more material hauled with light equipment); reduced settlement and stability problems; suitability for a wide variety of projects; potential frost mitigation from thermal insulation; potential for more uniform support, most important for pavements (p. 9-65). Potential disadvantages (4.1.2.2), as in the Lightweight Fill chapter: availability, which may not be local or regional and affects selection and cost; generally more expensive than other technologies except locally available recycled materials; leachate from some fills; durability, requiring protection or encapsulation of some materials; and geothermal properties that can cause differential icing (p. 9-66).
key_points: Except for locally available recycled materials, lightweight fill stabilization is typically more expensive than other technologies (p. 9-66).
sections.applicability: Weighing lightweight fill against other stabilization methods.

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Geotechnical, environmental and site feasibility of lightweight fill: subgrade sensitivity, strength and depth, groundwater (floating and water absorption), granular versus cohesive-behaving fills, leachate and pH, and consolidation of deep soft deposits.
sections.body: Geotechnical (4.1.3.1): sensitivity and strength of the subgrade and depth of soft deposits are key, with subgrade plasticity (expansive clay or frost heave); the groundwater table is especially critical since some materials float and several absorb moisture and gain weight when saturated (p. 9-66). Lightweight fills behave either like granular soils (wood fiber, blast furnace slag, boiler slag, fly ash, expanded shale, clay and slate (ESCS), tire shreds) or have an unconfined compressive strength and behave like cohesive soils in undrained loading (geofoam, cellular concrete). Environmental (4.1.3.2): groundwater for buoyancy and leachate; some fills can contaminate groundwater, deplete oxygen or change pH; disposal of excavated material. Site conditions (4.1.3.3): clearing and grubbing, stratigraphy, subgrade type, strength, stiffness and sensitivity, groundwater depth, topography for drainage, large consolidation settlement in deep soft deposits, on-site disposal (p. 9-67).
key_points: Granular-type fills: wood fiber, slags, fly ash, ESCS, tire shreds; strength-type fills: geofoam and cellular concrete (p. 9-66).
sections.applicability: Site screening for lightweight fill pavement stabilization.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: Limitations of lightweight fill stabilization: environmental concerns both ways, availability, cost and long-term performance of some materials, offset by the wide choice of materials.
sections.body: Limitations relate to environmental concerns (the fill's impact on the environment and the environment's effect on the fill), availability, cost and long-term performance of some materials (p. 9-67). With many materials to choose from, one will likely suit a given project.
sections.applicability: Recognizing limits on lightweight fill use.

sections.title: Construction and Materials
sections.summary: Construction and materials for lightweight fill stabilization, referring to the Lightweight Fill chapter: construction of lightweight fill: granular forms and chips placed in compacted layers, geofoam blocks or panels, foams or slurries in forms, compaction to maximize density without degradation, and volume reduction from compaction and loading.
sections.body: This section covers construction (4.2.1) and materials (4.2.2) for lightweight fill used in pavement stabilization (p. 9-67).
sections.applicability: Building lightweight fill stabilization layers.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Construction of lightweight fill: granular forms and chips placed in compacted layers, geofoam blocks or panels, foams or slurries in forms, compaction to maximize density without degradation, and volume reduction from compaction and loading.
sections.body: The Lightweight Fill chapter summarizes construction of each material, including placing, compacting and protecting against durability threats (p. 9-67). Granular forms (slag, fly ash, expanded shale) and chips (wood, tire shreds) are placed in layers and compacted; geofoam is placed in blocks or panels; some materials are placed as foams or slurries in forms. Compaction equipment is chosen to maximize density while preventing degradation, and volume reduction from compaction and shrinkage under soil cover and pavement is accounted for.
sections.applicability: Placing lightweight fill beneath pavements.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Lightweight fill materials used in highway construction, with their typical geotechnical design and construction parameters, composition and sources, are given in the Lightweight Fill chapter of the manual.
sections.body: An overview of common lightweight fill materials used in highway construction, with typical design and construction parameters and their composition and sources, is in the Lightweight Fill chapter earlier in the manual (p. 9-67).
sections.applicability: Finding lightweight fill material properties.

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.summary: Design overview for lightweight fill under pavements: design considerations, resilient modulus values (Table 9-9), design steps and references. Subsections cover: Design Considerations; Design Steps; Primary Design References.
sections.body: This section covers design considerations (4.3.1), design steps (4.3.2) and primary design references (4.3.3) for lightweight fill stabilization (p. 9-68).
sections.applicability: Designing pavements over lightweight fill.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Pavement design over lightweight fill: conventional fill procedures plus durability and other checks, little effect with at least 3 ft of gravel cover, resilient modulus as the key value (Table 9-9), a minimum 24 in. pavement system, and transition settlement gradient not over 1:200.
sections.body: Conventional fill design procedures apply to granular lightweight fills, plus checks of durability, water absorption, corrosion, combustion, erosion and environmental impacts (p. 9-68); NYSDOT (2015) covers tire shred compression, separation and combustion-preventing geometry; geofoam under pavements is covered in NCHRP Report 529 (Stark et al. 2004a) and Web Document 65 (Stark et al. 2004b). With a minimum of 3 feet of good quality gravel cover between pavement and lightweight material, the material has little impact on pavement design, even tire and geofoam; with thinner cover its support value must be determined. Resilient modulus is the most important value; CBR and subgrade reaction correlations are even more questionable than for soils, so laboratory resilient modulus tests are better. Table 9-9 (p. 9-69): geofoam (EPS) 1-2 pcf, CBR 2 to 4, MR 725-1450 psi; foamed concrete 20-62 pcf, CBR 15 to 150, E28 days 44-450 ksi; wood fiber 45-60 pcf, CBR 1, 1500 psi; tire shreds 45-60 pcf, 1/100 sand; ESCS 50-65 pcf, similar to gravel; fly ash 70-90 pcf, CBR 1 to 15 (Class C increases with time); boiler slag 50-65 pcf and air-cooled slag 70-94 pcf, CBR > 250, similar to or better than gravel. Field resilient modulus tests on the cover soil are ideal. A minimum pavement system thickness of 24 inches should be used above most lightweight fills other than durable gravel type fills. The transition to embankment soil should be gradual, with a calculated settlement gradient not exceeding 1:200 (vertical:horizontal).
key_points: At least 3 ft of good quality gravel cover makes the lightweight fill of little impact on pavement design (p. 9-68).
Resilient modulus is the most important pavement design value; lab resilient modulus tests are preferred.
Use a minimum pavement system thickness of 24 in. above most lightweight fills (p. 9-69).
Transition settlement gradient should not exceed 1:200 (vertical:horizontal).
Table 9-9: geofoam CBR 2 to 4 and MR 725-1450 psi; boiler and air-cooled slag CBR > 250.

sections.applicability: Assigning pavement support values to lightweight fill and detailing the cover and transitions.

sections.title: Design Steps
sections.summary: Design steps for lightweight fill stabilization: Section 2.3.2 thickness methods with increased thickness for CBR < 80 or the Giroud and Han method, proofrolling, blending (e.g., sand with at least 30% sand for tire chips), and NCHRP 529 geofoam design catalogs with a 24 in., 130 pcf preliminary dead load.
sections.body: The design steps of Section 2.3.2 apply to granular lightweight fill, but Figures 9-1 and 9-6 were developed for aggregates with CBR > 80, so thickness must be increased for lightweight aggregate with CBR < 80 or estimated by an alternate method (e.g., Giroud and Han in FHWA 2008); proofrolling should confirm the thickness (pp. 9-69 to 9-70). Granular lightweight fill is often blended with poorer soils; the modulus of tire chips is very low, but a sand-tire chip mixture (as low as 30% sand, Edil 2006) restores the modulus to about that of sand; Section 2.3.2.2 blending methods apply. Resilient modulus is the primary parameter for the layer and the equivalent stabilized subgrade. Class C fly ash is cementitious and can be used as an admixture (Section 6). For geofoam, NCHRP Report 529 and Web Document 65 give flexible and rigid design procedures: a low volume road catalog gives the structural number by EPS type, reliability and traffic, then AASHTO (1993) or state manuals set layer coefficients, with minimum AC and base thicknesses by ESALs; rigid catalogs give slab thickness by EPS type, reliability, ESALs, modulus of rupture and edge support/load transfer. For preliminary dead load use 24 inches thickness and 130 pcf (NCHRP 529).
key_points: Figures 9-1 and 9-6 assume aggregate CBR > 80; increase thickness for lightweight aggregate with lower CBR (p. 9-69).
A sand-tire chip mixture with as little as 30% sand restores modulus to about that of sand (Edil 2006) (p. 9-70).
Preliminary pavement dead load over geofoam: 24 in. at 130 pcf (NCHRP 529).

sections.summary: Specifications for lightweight fill under pavements follow the Lightweight Fill chapter, modified to require specified resilient modulus and durability, with FWD or LFWD performance monitoring.
sections.body: Specifications, quality assurance and monitoring for lightweight fill are covered in the Lightweight Fill chapter (p. 9-71). Typical specifications should be modified to require that materials meet the specified resilient modulus and durability requirements for pavement support. Performance monitoring could include FWD or LFWD testing to confirm compliance and gather data for future design. Specifications are on the GeoTechTools website.

sections.summary: Cost data for lightweight fill used in pavement subgrade stabilization are those given in the Lightweight Fill chapter, which apply equally here, with more information on GeoTechTools.
sections.body: Cost data in the Lightweight Fill chapter apply equally to lightweight fill for pavement subgrade stabilization; more information is on GeoTechTools (p. 9-71).

sections.title: Mechanical Stabilization: Recycled Materials
sections.summary: Recycled materials for subgrade stabilization: reuse of reclaimed asphalt pavement (RAP) and recycled concrete (RCP, RCM) as unbound aggregate, plus foundry sand; in-place recycling and slab fracturing used as base are excluded.
sections.body: Recycled materials for subgrade stabilization are of two forms: reuse of pavement materials themselves, and recycled waste materials as stabilizers or aggregate substitutes (p. 9-72). The first, the main use, is recycled concrete pavement (RCP) or reclaimed asphalt pavement (RAP) from the site or hauled in. The second involves mostly lightweight materials covered in Section 4; foundry sand and recycled concrete materials (RCM) from pavement and non-pavement projects are reviewed here. Of the asphalt recycling techniques (hot mix, hot in-place, cold mix, cold in-place, full depth reclamation), only removal and reuse of asphalt as unbound aggregate for subgrade stabilization is reviewed; in-place methods add foamed asphalt or emulsion and produce base or subbase. RAP is usually milled and pulverized. Concrete slab fracturing (crack and seat, break and seat, rubblization) produces in-place base and is not considered; poor subgrades often exclude these. RCP is crushed to sand and gravel sizes and is combined with other concrete as RCM. See FHWA-RD-97-148 (FHWA 1997a).
key_points: Only RAP and RCM used as unbound aggregate to stabilize subgrades, and foundry sand, are covered (p. 9-72).
Crack and seat, break and seat and rubblization produce base layers and are not considered for subgrade stabilization.
sections.applicability: Using recycled pavement materials and foundry sand as stabilization aggregate.

sections.title: Feasibility Considerations
sections.summary: Feasibility considerations for recycled materials in subgrade stabilization. Subsections cover: Applications; Advantages and Potential Disadvantages; Feasibility Evaluations; Limitations.
sections.body: This section covers applications, advantages and disadvantages, feasibility evaluations and limitations of recycled materials for subgrade stabilization (pp. 9-73 to 9-75).
sections.applicability: Screening recycled materials for stabilization.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Recycled pavement materials, on site or hauled in, provide a stabilization layer beneath the pavement section, and RAP and RCM may also give an improved base over marginal subgrades.
sections.body: Pavement materials are recycled on site or hauled from another site to give a stabilization layer where subgrade improvement is needed (p. 9-73). RAP and RCM may also provide an improved base course over marginal subgrades; base/subbase applications are covered in FHWA (1997a).
sections.applicability: Recycled stabilization layers beneath pavements.

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Advantages of RAP and RCM (lower reconstruction and disposal cost, aggregate conservation) and disadvantages (variability, contamination, low CBR of 100% RAP, leachate, tufa precipitates, freeze/thaw degradation and corrosion from high alkalinity and chlorides).
sections.body: Advantages (5.1.2.1): RAP or RCM can reduce reconstruction and waste disposal costs and conserve aggregates; properly designed and built, recycled-material pavements have performed as well as those with natural gravel (p. 9-73). Potential disadvantages (5.1.2.2): material is less uniform than quarried aggregate, though usually not a problem with good quality control; RAP may be commingled with contaminated base from over grinding or overzealous excavation; 100% RAP has a much lower CBR than gravel; residual oil and contamination may cause environmental issues, and some agencies require minimum separation from watercourses; crushed concrete can leach tufa-like precipitates (a white pasty substance from unhydrated cement) that can clog adjacent drains; RCM is susceptible to some freeze/thaw degradation, so freeze-thaw tests are needed within the frost zone; high alkalinity can corrode aluminum or galvanized steel pipes in the presence of moisture, worsened by chloride from deicing salts (p. 9-74).
key_points: 100% RAP has a much lower CBR than gravel (p. 9-73).
Tufa-like precipitates from unhydrated cement in RCM can clog adjacent drainage systems.
Perform freeze/thaw durability tests on RCM within the anticipated frost zone.
RCM alkalinity can corrode aluminum or galvanized steel pipes (p. 9-74).
sections.applicability: Weighing recycled aggregates for stabilization.

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Feasibility of recycled stabilization: same geotechnical issues as gravel and geosynthetics, groundwater and water bodies, subgrade strength to support grinding or rubblization equipment, dewatering, weather, noise and vibration, and the TRB E-C087 site evaluation (distress survey, pavement structure, soils).
sections.body: Geotechnical (5.1.3.1): the issues are practically the same as for thicker gravel or geosynthetics; identify groundwater and nearby water bodies (p. 9-74). For recycling the pavement on a project, subgrade type, quality (contamination) of in-place base and subbase and groundwater are key; the subgrade must support grinding or rubblization equipment; drains should be installed and the site dewatered before in-place recycling in wet, saturated conditions. Environmental considerations (printed also as 5.1.3.1): weather, since many processes use water and cold is a concern; wet weather while rubblizing or cracking concrete can disturb or destabilize the subgrade through pore pressure under impact; noise, vibration effects on nearby structures and dust; groundwater and runoff control. Site conditions (5.1.3.2): per TRB Circular E-C087 (TRB 2006), perform a distress survey (cracking, joint deficiencies, surface defects, miscellaneous), evaluate the pavement structure (layer types and thicknesses, shoulders) and determine soil conditions (types, bearing value such as CBR or Mr, moisture) (p. 9-75); otherwise the site conditions are as for thicker gravel, including clearing, water table, drainage, subgrade properties, disposal and consolidation of deep soft deposits.
key_points: Install drains and dewater before in-place recycling where soils are wet and saturated (p. 9-74).
TRB E-C087 evaluation: distress survey, existing pavement structure, and soil types, bearing value and moisture (p. 9-75).
sections.applicability: Evaluating a site for recycled material or in-place recycling.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: Limitations of recycling for stabilization: the fractured section must carry multiple equipment passes, in-place recycling may not be feasible on very soft (CBR <= 2) or highly sensitive subgrades, and high water must be addressed first.
sections.body: During in-place recycling the fractured pavement section must support multiple equipment passes (p. 9-75). In-place recycling may not be feasible where subgrade soils are very soft (e.g., CBR <= 2 based on the experience of several DOTs) or highly sensitive. High water levels should be addressed before in-place recycling.
key_points: In-place recycling may not be feasible on subgrades with CBR <= 2 or highly sensitive soils (p. 9-75).
sections.applicability: Recognizing where in-place recycling will not work.

sections.title: Construction and Materials
sections.summary: Construction and material controls for recycled aggregate stabilization layers: construction of recycled stabilization layers follows thick granular layer practice: soft ground equipment, a limit of a few inches of rutting, and functioning underdrains installed well ahead of recycling.
sections.body: This section covers construction (5.2.1) and materials (5.2.2) for recycled stabilization layers (p. 9-76).
sections.applicability: Building recycled aggregate stabilization layers.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Construction of recycled stabilization layers follows thick granular layer practice: soft ground equipment, a limit of a few inches of rutting, and functioning underdrains installed well ahead of recycling.
sections.body: Construction follows the thick granular layer practice: soft ground equipment (low ground pressure wide track dozers, extended backhoes and excavators, partially loaded dump trucks) to avoid disturbance; disturbance in sensitive soils can lead to significant overuse of gravel; equipment rutting the subgrade or granular layer more than a few inches should not operate (p. 9-76). Underdrains (installed or existing) should function, especially when recycling the existing pavement over weak subgrade or high water; install them as far in advance of recycling as possible; they also drain the section during rain.
sections.applicability: Placing recycled stabilization material and preparing drainage.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Material controls for RAP and RCM: gradation and density, steel removed, no oversized uncrushed pieces, RAP in RCM limited to 20%, fines control, washing to reduce tufa and salts, stockpile testing, standard compaction and subgrade strength checks.
sections.body: Gradation and density must be controlled for all recycling methods (p. 9-76). Reinforcing steel must be removed before RCM is crushed and screened. Uncrushed oversized pieces should not be placed, as they hinder uniform compaction or create voids. For composite pavements, RAP content in RCM should be limited to 20 percent to prevent loss of bearing strength and stiffness (FHWA 1997a). Fines (smaller than No. 200) must be controlled for drainage; washing may remove fines, dust, impurities and road salts, and washing RCM reduces tufa; only RCM without significant unhydrated cement or free lime should be used. Each stockpile should be tested (gradation, moisture, density, leach). Natural aggregate compaction requirements apply, using vibratory rollers. Subgrade strengths must be checked before and after recycling, and fines from intrusion or contaminated base minimized (p. 9-77).
key_points: Limit RAP content in RCM to 20% (FHWA 1997a) (p. 9-76).
Use only RCM without significant unhydrated cement or free lime, to control tufa.
Check subgrade strength before and after recycling (p. 9-77).
sections.applicability: Specifying recycled aggregate quality for stabilization.

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.summary: Design of RAP and RCM stabilization layers as for natural aggregates: laboratory resilient modulus, durability and drainage, FWD field trials, and corrosion and environmental checks.
sections.body: Design requirements for RAP and RCM aggregates are essentially those of natural aggregates, evaluated against the property requirements of the material they replace (p. 9-77). Pavement support values (resilient modulus) should be determined from laboratory tests, with durability and drainage assessed; FWD field trials to confirm as-constructed properties are recommended. Durability is critical for many of these materials, and corrosion potential (especially RCM) and environmental impacts must be assessed.
key_points: Determine the pavement support value from laboratory tests and confirm with FWD field trials (p. 9-77).
sections.applicability: Designing stabilization layers of recycled aggregates.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Design considerations for recycled stabilization: lab properties for hauled-in RCM, RAP and foundry sand versus field sampling for recycled existing pavements; RAP CBR 20 to 25%, RCM CBR 90 to more than 140%, foundry sand CBR about 4 to 20 and Mr about 6,000 to 30,000 psi.
sections.body: Hauled-in RCM, RAP and foundry sand can be treated as aggregate with laboratory design properties as QC/QA targets; for recycling existing pavements, design relies on lab testing during crushing or field sampling, in situ tests and test pits, and a thorough subgrade investigation to decide whether rubblization is possible (p. 9-77). Recycled asphalt (5.3.1.1): RAP often screens only to a 2 inch maximum size; contaminated base removed with it can spoil hydraulic properties; CBR is typically 20 to 25 percent with about 10 times greater plastic strains than natural aggregate (Edil 2011); blends with 40% RAP have exceeded CBR 150 after 1 week (FHWA 1997a) (p. 9-78). Recycled concrete (5.3.1.2): RCM is highly angular with CBR 90 to more than 140 percent, comparable to crushed limestone; pH greater than 11 can corrode aluminum or galvanized steel; drains through or beside the layer should allow for tufa, with open graded gravel designed as a filter for the RCM adjacent to it and no geotextile across that interface. Waste recycled material (5.3.1.3): foundry sand (clay or chemically bonded mold sand) has CBR about 4 to 20 and Mr about 6,000 to 30,000 psi, generally equal to or better than subbase, a very good stabilization aggregate (Edil 2006); strict moisture control is needed because of bentonite; above about 6% bentonite the compacted sand may be rather impermeable and could serve as a partial encapsulation cover, verified by permeability tests (p. 9-79).
key_points: RAP: CBR typically 20 to 25%, about 10 times greater plastic strains than natural aggregate (Edil 2011) (p. 9-77).
RCM: CBR 90 to more than 140%, pH greater than 11 (p. 9-78).
No geotextile filter across the RCM-drain gravel interface because of tufa.
Foundry sand: CBR about 4 to 20, Mr about 6,000 to 30,000 psi; above about 6% bentonite it may be rather impermeable (pp. 9-78 to 9-79).
sections.applicability: Assigning design properties to RAP, RCM and foundry sand stabilization layers.

sections.title: Design Steps
sections.summary: Design steps for recycled stabilization: Section 2.3.2 for aggregate replacement, Section 3.3.2 with geotextiles, increased thickness for recycled material with CBR < 80 or the Giroud and Han method, proof rolling, and FHWA (1997b) for in-place recycling.
sections.body: If the recycled material simply replaces aggregate, the design steps of Section 2.3.2 apply; with geotextiles, Section 3.3.2 (p. 9-79). If the design charts are used (printed as Figures 9-2 or 9-7), an increased stabilization layer thickness is required for recycled material with CBR < 80; alternatively the Giroud and Han method in FHWA (2008) takes the material CBR as an input. Proof rolling should confirm thickness. For in-place recycling, step-by-step procedures are in FHWA (1997b).
key_points: Increase stabilization thickness for recycled material with CBR < 80 when using the design charts (p. 9-79).
sections.applicability: Sizing recycled aggregate stabilization layers.

sections.title: Primary Design References
sections.summary: Primary design references for recycled materials: FHWA (1997a) waste and byproduct guidelines, ARRA (2001) Basic Asphalt Recycling Manual and FHWA (1997b) pavement recycling guidelines.
sections.body: References (p. 9-79): FHWA (1997a), User Guidelines for Waste and Byproduct Materials in Pavement Construction (Chesner, Collins and MacKay, FHWA-RD-97-148); Asphalt Recycling and Reclaiming Association (ARRA) (2001), Basic Asphalt Recycling Manual; FHWA (1997b), Pavement Recycling Guidelines for State and Local Governments (Kandhal and Mallick, FHWA-SA-98-042).
sections.applicability: Finding design sources for recycled pavement materials.

sections.title: Overview of Construction Specifications and Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Specifications, quality assurance and monitoring for recycled aggregate stabilization layers. Subsections cover: Specification Development; Summary of Quality Assurance; Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control.
sections.body: This section covers specification development (5.4.1), quality assurance (5.4.2) and monitoring and construction control (5.4.3) for recycled stabilization (p. 9-79).
sections.applicability: Specifying and checking recycled stabilization layers.

sections.title: Specification Development
sections.summary: Specifications for RAP and RCP aggregates: state DOT aggregate specifications, the FHWA (1997a) user guidelines, and two university research center specifications (Edil 2011) with operator requirements for supply, compliance, safety and quality.
sections.body: RAP and RCP aggregates are essentially natural aggregates and most state DOTs have material, placement and compaction specifications (p. 9-79). FHWA (1997a) contains a Users Guideline section for RAP, RCM and other recycled fills (processing, properties, design, construction including cold weather and corrosion mitigation, unresolved issues); it and state specifications are reviewed in GeoTechTools (p. 9-80). A university recycled materials research center published two specifications for RAP and RCP as unbound road base (Edil 2011): a standard specification for grading requirements and density determination of RAP as unbound base and subbase (in ASTM balloting) and a standard guide for recycled aggregates as unbound roadbase (in draft). The guide assumes the operator (1) secures, stockpiles, crushes, tests and stockpiles the product; (2) complies with solid waste rules; (3) complies with air quality rules; (4) has worker health, safety and environmental plans; (5) meets recycled aggregate quality standards.
sections.applicability: Writing specifications for recycled stabilization aggregates.

sections.title: Summary of Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Quality control of recycled stabilization: moisture, density or stiffness and thickness, random stockpile sampling, segregation monitoring, GPS with point checks, DCP and proof rolling.
sections.body: As with gravel, primary quality control is moisture, density or stiffness and thickness (p. 9-80). Each recycled source differs, so random samples of stockpiles should be taken and stockpiling and handling monitored for segregation. GPS with point checks controls thickness; the DCP gives strength and effective depth; proof rolling evaluates deformation and rutting potential.
sections.applicability: Field quality checks on recycled aggregate layers.

sections.title: Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control
sections.summary: FWD testing from the surface of the improved layer measures layer and subgrade stiffness after in-place recycling, confirms design resilient modulus and gives a reference for long-term monitoring.
sections.body: The FWD test on the surface of the improved layer measures the stiffness of that layer and of the subgrade after in-place recycling (p. 9-81). Resilient modulus from FWD results confirms the design requirements and provides a reference for future FWD on the new pavement surface for long-term performance monitoring.
sections.applicability: Verifying recycled stabilization layers by FWD.

sections.title: Cost Data
sections.summary: Recycled pavement materials for stabilization are typically incorporated in highway reconstruction as subbase/base aggregate or roadbed embankment material.
sections.body: For stabilization applications, recycled pavement materials are typically incorporated into a highway reconstruction project, as aggregate in subbase/base courses or as roadbed embankment material (p. 9-81).
sections.applicability: Context for recycled material costs.

sections.title: Cost Components
sections.summary: Recycled material costs: specifications should allow but not force recycled materials; preliminary budgets should include a nominal saving of $2.00 to $5.00 per ton of recycled material used onsite, except very large projects over 100,000 tons.
sections.body: Specifications should allow the use of recycled materials but not force it, letting market forces set the most cost effective and sustainable use (p. 9-81). Availability of alternatives and demand from other markets strongly influence savings passed to the owner, making them hard to quantify. Except for very large projects (greater than 100,000 tons of available recycled material) where savings may be significant, preliminary budgets should include a nominal saving of $2.00 to $5.00 per ton of recycled material incorporated onsite. More cost information is on GeoTechTools.
key_points: Budget a nominal saving of $2.00 to $5.00 per ton of recycled material incorporated onsite (p. 9-81).
sections.applicability: Budgeting recycled material use in reconstruction.

sections.title: Admixture/Chemical Stabilization
sections.summary: Admixture (chemical) stabilization of pavement subgrades with cement, cement kiln dust, lime, fly ash, asphalt and combinations: overview of each admixture and a generic procedure for the optimum admixture content.
sections.body: A variety of admixtures can be mixed with the subgrade to improve its performance (p. 9-82). The section gives a general overview of each admixture and a generalized outline for determining the optimum admixture content, with references for the design details of each method.
sections.applicability: Chemical treatment of weak, plastic or wet pavement subgrades.

sections.title: Feasibility Considerations
sections.summary: Feasibility considerations for admixture stabilization: applications, advantages and disadvantages, geotechnical, environmental and site evaluations, limitations and alternatives.
sections.body: This section covers applications (6.1.1), advantages and disadvantages (6.1.2), feasibility evaluations (6.1.3), limitations (6.1.4) and alternatives (6.1.5) for admixture stabilization (pp. 9-82 to 9-88).
sections.applicability: Screening a subgrade for chemical stabilization.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Applications of admixtures for soft, compressible, expansive and wet soils, the Austroads guide to selecting an admixture (Figure 9-8), cementing agents that bond particles and cut capillary passages, and caution with lime and lime-fly ash on clays in seasonal frost areas.
sections.body: Figure 9-8 (Austroads 1998) shows the admixture types with initial guidance on their application; forms of stabilization may be combined (e.g., lime to dry and reduce plasticity before another method), and miscellaneous chemicals are a broad guideline only (p. 9-82). Admixtures stabilize soft and/or compressible, expansive and wet soils (p. 9-83). Cementing agents (Portland cement, bitumen, lime, cement kiln dust and lime-fly ash) bond particles and partially remove capillary passages, reducing moisture movement. Care is needed with lime and lime-fly ash on clay soils in seasonal frost areas. For expansive soils, stabilization means treatment with bitumen, Portland cement, slaked or hydrated lime and fly ash to limit volume change; chemical stabilization can substantially increase strength.
key_points: Take care using lime and lime-fly ash with clay soils in seasonal frost areas (p. 9-83).
figures: Figure 9-8: Guide for selection of admixture stabilization method(s).
sections.applicability: Choosing an admixture type from soil grading and plasticity.

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Advantages of admixtures (in-place treatment, stiffer subgrade, lower plasticity, swell and compressibility) and disadvantages (curing of several days to a week, lab testing, field control, dust and weather, lime or fly ash raising frost susceptibility, sulfate heave).
sections.body: Advantages (6.1.2.1): in-place treatment eliminates over excavated spoil and its disposal and replacement; admixtures increase subgrade stiffness; they reduce plasticity, water absorption, swelling potential and compressibility and increase strength and modulus with time; lime reduces swell of expansive soil depending on clay mineral activity; admixtures exist for most soil types (p. 9-83). Potential disadvantages (6.1.2.2): curing of several days and often up to one week is needed, and adequate curing is important; up front lab testing and very good field control are needed for a uniform, long lasting product; dust control and weather dependency. Some admixture (e.g., lime or fly ash) treatment can turn a soil of negligible to moderate frost heave into a highly frost susceptible one, acting more like silt; for lime this was reported as caused by insufficient curing. For lime, CKD and possibly cement, soil sulfates can react with free lime to form expansive minerals and swelling where none existed (p. 9-84).
key_points: Admixtures usually need a curing time of several days, often up to one week (p. 9-83).
Lime or fly ash treatment can make a soil highly frost susceptible, reported for lime as due to insufficient curing.
Sulfates can react with free lime from lime, CKD and possibly cement to form expansive minerals (p. 9-84).
sections.applicability: Weighing chemical stabilization against other methods.

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Feasibility checks for admixtures: cement needs PI < 20 and at least 45% passing No. 40, 3 to 10% cement and 150 psi in 7 days; lime 3 to 8% and 50 psi in 28 days with PI about 10 as the lower limit; state agency selection charts (Figures 9-9 to 9-11).
sections.body: Geotechnical (6.1.3.1): applicability is in Table 9-2 and Figure 9-8 (p. 9-84). Cement mixing requires PI less than 20 and a minimum of 45% passing the No. 40 sieve, though highly plastic clays pretreated with lime or fly ash may later take cement; for granular and/or nonplastic soils the cement content should be 3 to 10% of dry soil weight with an unconfined compressive strength of at least 150 psi within 7 days; cement per AASHTO M 85; compact to a minimum 95% of AASHTO T 134. For lime on clay or highly plastic clayey soils, lime content should be 3 to 8% of dry weight with at least 50 psi unconfined strength within 28 days; optimum lime from unconfined strength and Atterberg limits of trial mixes, with pH giving an initial near-optimum value; pozzolanic gain depends on available silica and alumina; a plasticity index of about 10 is commonly the lower limit for inorganic clays; compact to 95% of AASHTO T 99. Pozzolanic fly ash suits cohesive and granular materials; asphalt suits silty, sandy and granular materials. Environmental (6.1.3.2): dust control and weather. Site conditions (6.1.3.3): Figure 9-9 (Ohio DOT 2002) and Figures 9-10 and 9-11 (after Jones et al. 2010) summarize the site conditions two state agencies use for selection; evaluate classification, moisture, plasticity, sulfate content, organic content and strength, and the water table, since high water may need dewatering (pp. 9-85 to 9-87).
key_points: Cement: PI < 20, at least 45% passing No. 40, 3 to 10% cement, 150 psi within 7 days, 95% of AASHTO T 134 (p. 9-84).
Lime: 3 to 8% lime, at least 50 psi within 28 days, 95% of AASHTO T 99.
A plasticity index of about 10 is commonly the lower limit for lime stabilization of inorganic clays.
Evaluate classification, moisture, plasticity, sulfates, organics, strength and water table (p. 9-87).
figures: Figure 9-9: Site conditions for considering cement or lime stabilization.
Figure 9-10: Selecting a first-level project subgrade stabilization strategy.
Figure 9-11: Selection of stabilization strategy for sulfate-rich soils.
sections.applicability: Checking whether cement or lime suits a subgrade soil.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: Limitations of admixtures: soils too soft for mixing equipment (CBR < 1), stabilization generally not required when PI < 12 and R > 20, no cementitious or pozzolanic stabilization above 8000 ppm sulfate, special strategies above 3000 ppm, and reduced effect with organics.
sections.body: A main limitation is soils too soft to support mixing equipment (p. 9-87). If PI is less than 12 and R > 20, stabilization is generally not required; if CBR < 1 (R < 1) the subgrade will likely not support mixing equipment and other technologies (geosynthetics, lightweight fill) should be considered. The other primary limitation is sulfates: cementitious and pozzolanic stabilization should not be used when soil sulfate content exceeds 8000 ppm (Figure 9-10), and special strategies are needed above 3000 ppm (Figure 9-11), with swell tests. Organics reduce the effectiveness of cementitious and pozzolanic methods, requiring significant increases in quantity if they work at all (p. 9-88).
key_points: Stabilization is generally not required if PI < 12 and R > 20 (p. 9-87).
With CBR < 1 the subgrade likely will not support admixture mixing equipment.
No cementitious or pozzolanic stabilization above 8000 ppm sulfate; special strategies and swell tests above 3000 ppm.
sections.applicability: Recognizing soils where chemical stabilization should not be used.

sections.title: Alternative Solutions (or Technologies)
sections.summary: Alternatives to admixtures: more gravel, geosynthetics with gravel, dewatering, lightweight fill for soils too soft for admixtures, and partial encapsulation for swelling soils.
sections.body: More gravel, geosynthetics with gravel and/or dewatering are standard alternatives to admixtures for weak soils (p. 9-88). Geosynthetics and lightweight fill are especially effective where soils are too soft for admixtures. For swelling soils, partial encapsulation could be considered (printed as covered in Section 8 Moisture Control).
sections.applicability: Choosing a non-chemical alternative.

sections.title: Construction and Materials
sections.summary: Construction steps and admixture materials for chemical stabilization: construction of chemical stabilization: delivery and distribution, mixing (poor mixing the leading cause of failure), compaction and curing above 40°F for 3 to 7 days; dry hydrated lime, quicklime or slurry; two-stage mixing for plastic clays; lime lowering maximum density.
sections.body: This section covers construction (6.2.1) and the admixture materials: cement and CKD, lime, fly ash, asphalt and combinations (6.2.2) (pp. 9-88 to 9-94).
sections.applicability: Building chemically stabilized subgrades.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Construction of chemical stabilization: delivery and distribution, mixing (poor mixing the leading cause of failure), compaction and curing above 40°F for 3 to 7 days; dry hydrated lime, quicklime or slurry; two-stage mixing for plastic clays; lime lowering maximum density.
sections.body: The basic steps are (1) pozzolan delivery and distribution, (2) mixing, (3) compacting and (4) curing (p. 9-88). Pozzolans are applied dry or as slurry; dry hydrated lime is very fine and dusty, quicklime granular and much less dusty. Material is spread by hand from bags, pneumatic trucks with spreader bars or dump trucks with controlled tailgates; lime slurry is mixed centrally or in portable systems, typically 1 ton of lime with 500 gallons of water giving a slurry with 31% lime solids (TRB 1987; the printed text says 600 tons of slurry). Adequate mixing is critical; poor mixing is the leading cause of unsatisfactory results; soils are mixed by disking, repeated blading or traveling rotary or pug-mill mixers, in thin lifts with multiple passes. Highly plastic materials may be mixed in two stages, the reduced plasticity after several days of curing aiding final mixing. Compaction follows standard procedures, but lime generally decreases maximum density and increases optimum water content, so compaction curves of the in situ mixture may be needed for control (p. 9-89). Curing above 40°F with adequate moisture is essential for pozzolanic strength gain; 3 to 7 days is typical, with moist curing or an asphalt seal. Final evaluation is by proof rolling, DCP and/or FWD.
key_points: Poor mixing is the leading cause of unsatisfactory stabilization results (p. 9-88).
Lime generally lowers maximum density and raises optimum water content; use compaction curves of the in situ mixture (p. 9-89).
Cure above 40°F with adequate moisture; a 3 to 7 day cure is typical.
sections.applicability: Field construction of lime, cement and fly ash treated subgrades.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Admixture materials: cement types I, IA, II and III and CKD with organic (pH at least 12.0 test) and sulfate (avoid cement above about 1% sulfate in fine soils) concerns; hydrated lime, quicklime and dolomitic limes (Figure 9-12); Class C and F fly ash; asphalt emulsions; and lime-cement, lime-asphalt and lime-fly ash combinations.
sections.body: Cement and CKD (6.2.2.1): Type I and Type IA gave about the same results; Type II has largely replaced Type I for sulfate resistance at the same cost; Type III gives higher strength in some soils; specifications in ASTM C150 (p. 9-89). Low molecular weight organics (nucleic acid, dextrose) retard hydration; if the pH of a 10:1 soil-cement mix 15 minutes after mixing is at least 12.0, organics probably will not interfere. Sulfate-clay reactions can deteriorate fine-grained soil-cement while granular soil-cements appear resistant; cement for fine-grained soils with more than about 1% sulfate should be avoided; for CKD report sulfate content, test soils for sulfate minerals (often gypsum) and run swell tests (p. 9-90). Lime (6.2.2.2): hydrated lime Ca(OH)2, quicklime CaO and dolomitic forms; hydrated lime is most common in the US, quicklime growing; effects shown in Figure 9-12 (p. 9-91). Hydration dries the soil; Ca+2 and Mg+2 exchange with Na+ and K+, reducing plasticity, swell and shrinkage and improving workability; agglomeration coarsens texture; these effects occur usually within 1 hour with thorough mixing (p. 9-92). Fly ash (6.2.2.3): Class C self-cementing, Class F needs lime; must meet ASTM C593. Asphalt (6.2.2.4): for silty, sandy and granular soils, used up to PI 15 but more commonly on sandy, well-graded low-fines soils; not appropriate in poorly drained areas; in-place work uses emulsions rather than cutbacks (p. 9-93). Combinations (6.2.2.5): lime first to reduce clay plasticity for cement or asphalt; lime-asphalt needs about 1 to 2 percent lime as an anti-stripping agent; in lime-fly ash the matrix (fly ash, lime, minus No. 4 fines) should 'float' the coarse aggregate, about 2 percent above the optimum fines content (p. 9-94).
key_points: If the pH of a 10:1 soil-cement mix is at least 12.0 after 15 minutes, organics probably will not interfere with hardening (p. 9-89).
Avoid cement for fine-grained soils with more than about 1% sulfate (p. 9-90).
Lime drying, plasticity reduction and texture changes usually occur within 1 hour of thorough mixing (p. 9-92).
Lime-asphalt: about 1 to 2 percent lime; lime-fly ash matrix about 2 percent above optimum fines content (pp. 9-93 to 9-94).
figures: Figure 9-12: Examples of the effects of lime stabilization on various soils.
sections.applicability: Selecting and qualifying cement, lime, fly ash and asphalt admixtures.

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.summary: Design overview for admixture stabilization: binder selection and a generic mix design procedure. Subsections cover: Design Considerations (Chemical/Binder Selection); Design Steps; Primary Design References.
sections.body: This section covers design considerations for chemical and binder selection (6.3.1), generic design steps (6.3.2) and primary design references (6.3.3) (pp. 9-94 to 9-96).
sections.applicability: Designing chemically stabilized subgrades.

sections.title: Design Considerations (Chemical/Binder Selection)
sections.summary: Admixture design depends on the purpose (reduce moisture, reduce plasticity, improve strength) with special consideration of sulfate, organic, pH and chloride contents; Jones et al. (2010) give detailed steps.
sections.body: Design of the admixture depends on the purpose of stabilization: reducing moisture content, reducing plasticity or improving strength (p. 9-94). Special consideration must be given to the sulfate content, organic content, pH and chloride content of the soil, which could affect performance and durability. Jones et al. (2010) provides detailed design steps for each issue.
sections.applicability: Choosing a binder for a stabilization purpose.

sections.title: Design Steps
sections.summary: Generic nine-step mix design for lime, cement, lime-fly ash, lime-cement-fly ash or asphalt: classify, select admixture and trial mixes (lime at pH about 12.4 in 1 hour), moisture-density, cured triplicates, strength, resilient modulus, freeze-thaw, select content, and add 0.5 to 1%.
sections.body: For improving subgrade strength the design is generic to lime, cement, lime-fly ash, lime-cement-fly ash or asphalt (p. 9-94). Step 1: classify the soil (% < No. 200, % < No. 40, PI, sulfate content). Step 2: select admixture(s) (Table 9-2, Figures 9-9 to 9-12) and prepare trial mixes (FHWA 2010, JDAAF 1994, Jones et al. 2010): lime, select the lowest % with pH about 12.4 in 1 hour; cement, estimate content from a table; asphalt, use the equation and table in FHWA 2010 or JDAAF 1994 (p. 9-95). Step 3: develop the moisture-density relationship. Step 4: prepare triplicate samples cured at the specified density (e.g., 90% AASHTO T 180 or ASTM D1557) at optimum water and admixture contents several points above and below. Step 5: index strength, unconfined compressive strength (ASTM D5102 or AASHTO T 208) for lime and cement, Marshall Stability (ASTM D6927 or AASHTO T 245) for asphalt. Step 6: resilient modulus (e.g., AASHTO T 307) at the optimum, tested or correlated. Step 7: freeze-thaw tests as regionally required for cement, cement-fly ash, lime-cement-fly ash. Step 8: select the percent meeting minimum design strength and freeze-thaw durability. Step 9: add 0.5 to 1% to compensate for non-uniform mixing.
key_points: Lime trial: select the lowest % giving pH about 12.4 in 1 hour (p. 9-94).
Cure triplicate specimens at the specified density, e.g., 90% AASHTO T 180 (p. 9-95).
Add 0.5 to 1% admixture to compensate for non-uniform mixing.
sections.applicability: Running a laboratory mix design for a chemically stabilized subgrade.

sections.title: Primary Design References
sections.summary: Primary design references for admixture stabilization: JDAAF (1994) TM 5-822-14, FHWA (2010), Jones et al. (2010), National Lime Association (2004), Portland Cement Association (1995), American Coal Ash Association (1991) and Asphalt Institute (1979).

sections.title: Overview of Construction Specifications and Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Specifications, quality assurance and monitoring for chemically stabilized subgrades. Subsections cover: Specification Development; Summary of Quality Assurance; Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control.
sections.body: This section covers specification development (6.4.1), quality assurance (6.4.2) and monitoring and construction control (6.4.3) for admixture stabilization (pp. 9-96 to 9-97).
sections.applicability: Specifying and checking chemical stabilization.

sections.title: Specification Development
sections.summary: Combined performance and method specifications for chemical stabilization: acceptance criteria, contractor qualifications and responsibilities, resilient modulus and durability requirements, and an outline from grade correction and test strip to curing and trafficking.
sections.body: Combined performance and method approach specifications are used for most chemical stabilization projects (p. 9-96). They should include acceptance criteria and minimum contractor qualifications, state the contractor's responsibility for material selection, mix design and quality control, identify equipment and construction methods, and define the engineer's responsibility for mix design verification and quality assurance. Stabilized materials should meet specified resilient modulus and durability requirements; sulfate-rich and organic soils need special considerations. General requirements: grade correction, test strip, mixing and application equipment, mixing crew responsibilities, mixing depth and moisture content, mellowing before compaction (lime), compaction, compaction quality control, curing and trafficking (p. 9-97). All vehicles should be kept off the stabilized layer during the curing period and/or until the minimum specified strength is reached.
key_points: Keep all vehicles off the stabilized layer during curing and/or until the minimum specified strength is achieved (p. 9-97).
sections.applicability: Writing specifications for chemical subgrade stabilization.

sections.title: Summary of Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Quality assurance of chemical stabilization: agency mix design verification, measurement of thickness, moisture, stabilizer content, compaction and delay, curing, gradation, strength and modulus, and blend uniformity checked in test holes with phenolphthalein for lime and cement.
sections.body: The agency should verify the mix design and conduct quality assurance unless the contract assigns it to others (p. 9-97). Critical parameters are thickness of the stabilized layer, moisture content, stabilizer content, compaction effort and delay, curing procedures and time, gradation of the mixture, shear strength and modulus. Blend uniformity is one of the more important measures: dig holes across the roadway and check for uniform consistency, color and moisture, sampling for moisture and, if possible, stabilizer content. For cement and lime, spraying the hole sides with phenolphthalein gives a quick check; the soil should turn a uniform deep red, indicating sufficient stabilizer.
key_points: Phenolphthalein sprayed in test holes should turn lime or cement treated soil a uniform deep red (p. 9-97).
sections.applicability: Field quality checks on chemically treated subgrades.

sections.title: Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control
sections.summary: Monitoring chemical stabilization: thickness and uniformity from test holes, DCP and ground penetrating radar (ASTM D6432), and FWD or LFWD backcalculated resilient modulus for compliance and long-term reference.
sections.body: Thickness and blend uniformity are best measured with test holes along and across the alignment, complemented by DCP and/or ground penetrating radar (GPR, ASTM D6432) (p. 9-97). Performance monitoring could include FWD or LFWD to confirm design compliance and gather data; the backcalculated resilient modulus confirms design requirements and is a reference for future FWD on the new pavement surface.
sections.applicability: Verifying chemically stabilized layers.

sections.title: Cost Components
sections.summary: Chemical stabilization costs (2007 to 2010 data): subgrade modification pay item by the square yard at $2 to $5 (printed per cubic yard) for projects over 10,000 yd2; cement and lime $100 to $150/ton over 150 tons; fly ash $40 to $80/ton over 350 tons; mixing plant mobilization about $25,000.
sections.body: Typical pay items are subgrade modification by the square yard (equipment, labor and incidentals to mix, compact and fine grade) and cement, fly ash or lime by the ton (p. 9-98). Bid prices for subgrade modification on projects over 10,000 yd2 range from $2 to $5 (printed as per cubic yard). Material prices: cement $100 to $150 per ton for quantities > 150 tons; fly ash $40 to $80 per ton for > 350 tons; lime $100 to $150 per ton for > 150 tons. Most equipment is common to highway work so added mobilization is negligible, except an on-site plant for a chemically modified base, about $25,000 to mobilize. Cost ranges are based on 2007 through 2010 data; see GeoTechTools.
key_points: Cement and lime $100 to $150 per ton (> 150 tons); fly ash $40 to $80 per ton (> 350 tons) (p. 9-98).
Mobilization of an on-site mixing plant is about $25,000.
